Chapter 9 — Kernel Functions and the Representer Theorem

Chapters 6 and 8 ended on the same observation: the dual form of ridge regression and the dual form of the support vector machine use the training examples only through their inner products. This chapter follows that observation to its conclusion. If we can compute the inner product of two feature vectors without ever building them, the feature space can be enormous, or even infinite-dimensional, and the cost of the method does not depend on its dimension. We shall characterize the functions that are inner products (the positive semidefinite kernels), prove the representer theorem, which says that the solution of a very large class of penalized problems is a combination of kernel functions centered at the training points, derive kernel ridge regression, use the SVM of Chapter 8 with the Gaussian kernel, and see how to approximate a kernel method when nnn is too large for it.

9.1 Learning objectives¶

Section 6.7 improved linear models by adding nonlinear features (all the monomials up to a given degree), and found a limit: the number of features grows quickly with the degree and with the number of inputs, and a fit with many features is a disaster without regularization. Section 6.7.2 and Chapter 8 showed that the computation can be moved to the dual, where the cost depends on nnn and not on the number of features. The remaining step is to stop building the features at all.

After working through the chapter you will be able to:

  1. define a kernel as an inner product in a feature space, and write the polynomial, Gaussian (RBF), Laplacian and linear kernels, together with the distances and angles that a kernel defines;

  2. state and prove the characterization of kernels (a symmetric function is a kernel if and only if all its Gram matrices are positive semidefinite) and the closure properties (sums, products, exponentials), and use them to show that the Gaussian kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature space, which you can write explicitly in one dimension;

  3. check numerically that a function is, or is not, a kernel, and explain what can go wrong with a function that is not (the dual problem is no longer convex);

  4. define the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a kernel, state and prove the representer theorem, and use it to turn a penalized problem over functions into a problem in nnn coefficients;

  5. derive kernel ridge regression, show that it reduces to the ridge regression of Chapter 6 for the linear kernel, prove the leave-one-out shortcut for it, and read the shrinkage of the eigenvalues of the Gram matrix as the shrinkage of the singular values of Section 6.3.2;

  6. use the kernel SVM (the SMO of Section 8.5.2 works on any Gram matrix), tune (C,γ)(C, \gamma)(C,γ) with the protocols of Chapter 5, and describe the three regimes of the bandwidth γ\gammaγ: a nearly linear model, a good fit, and memorization;

  7. bound the generalization of a kernel classifier through the norm ∥f∥H\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}∥f∥H​ and the radius sup⁡xk(x,x)\sup_x\sqrt{k(x, x)}supx​k(x,x)​ (Theorem 3.7 in the feature space);

  8. approximate a kernel with random Fourier features (prove that they are unbiased and give a Hoeffding bound) or with the Nyström method, and say when the approximation is worth it.

Prerequisites. Chapters 1 to 8. In particular feature maps and the dual form of ridge regression (Sections 6.7.1 and 6.7.2), the singular-value view of ridge (Section 6.3.2) and its leave-one-out shortcut (Proposition 6.8), the margin and Rademacher bounds of Section 3.8, the dual of the SVM and the function smo (Sections 8.2 to 8.5), and the cross-validation protocols of Chapter 5. Linear algebra of symmetric positive semidefinite matrices (Section 2.3.7) is used throughout.

A word about the data in this chapter

The experiments use real data sets, all shipped with scikit-learn: Iris (the Gram matrices of Section 9.3), Breast Cancer (the stratified split of Chapters 6 to 8, 426 training and 143 test patients, malignant =+1= +1=+1), Digits (the stratified split of 1347 training and 450 test images) and Diabetes (the 331/111 split of Chapters 6 and 7). Only one example is not data: the three points of Worked example 9.1, small enough to be solved by hand. The features of the Breast Cancer data are standardized with the statistics of the training set, as in Chapter 8; for Digits we shall see that the scale of the features matters for kernels more than for linear models.

9.2 From inner products to kernels¶

9.2.1 The idea¶

Three formulas that we already know have the same structure. The ridge regression of Section 6.7.2, written in the dual, predicts with f^(x)=∑iαi φ(xi)⊤φ(x)\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i\alpha_i\,\boldsymbol\varphi(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top\boldsymbol\varphi(\mathbf{x})f^​(x)=∑i​αi​φ(xi​)⊤φ(x) and α=(ΦΦ⊤+λI)−1y\boldsymbol\alpha = (\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Phi^\top + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y}α=(ΦΦ⊤+λI)−1y. The soft-margin SVM of Theorem 8.4 maximizes ∑iαi−12∑i,jαiαjyiyj xi⊤xj\sum_i\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j∑i​αi​−21​∑i,j​αi​αj​yi​yj​xi⊤​xj​ and predicts with sign⁡(∑iαiyi xi⊤x+b)\operatorname{sign}\big(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x} + b\big)sign(∑i​αi​yi​xi⊤​x+b). And the SMO algorithm of Section 8.5.2 touched the data only through the Gram matrix. In all of them, if the data are first mapped to feature vectors ϕ(x)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x})ϕ(x), the features enter only through the inner products ϕ(x)⊤ϕ(z)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x})^\top\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})ϕ(x)⊤ϕ(z).

Definition 9.1 (kernel)

A function k:X×X→Rk:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}k:X×X→R is a kernel if there exist a real vector space F\mathcal{F}F with an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle⟨⋅,⋅⟩ (a feature space, finite- or infinite-dimensional, complete) and a map ϕ:X→F\boldsymbol\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{F}ϕ:X→F such that

k(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩for all x,z.k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) = \langle\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\rangle\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}.k(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩for all x,z.
(1)

The kernel trick consists in replacing xi⊤xj\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jxi⊤​xj​ by k(xi,xj)k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)k(xi​,xj​) in an algorithm that uses the data only through inner products: the algorithm then runs in the feature space, without ever computing ϕ\boldsymbol\phiϕ.

The matrix K∈Rn×n\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}K∈Rn×n with entries Kij=k(xi,xj)K_{ij} = k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)Kij​=k(xi​,xj​) is the Gram matrix of the sample (the kernel matrix). The cost of a kernel method depends on nnn, through K\mathbf{K}K, and on the cost of evaluating kkk, but not on the dimension of F\mathcal{F}F. This is what makes it possible to use feature spaces of dimension 105 or infinite. Here are the kernels that we shall use (γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0, c≥0c\ge 0c≥0 and the integer p≥1p\ge 1p≥1 are parameters):

Kernelk(x,z)k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})k(x,z)Feature space
Linearx⊤z\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z}x⊤zRd\mathbb{R}^dRd, ϕ(x)=x\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}ϕ(x)=x
Polynomial(γ x⊤z+c)p(\gamma\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + c)^p(γx⊤z+c)pall the monomials of degree ≤p\le p≤p (for c>0c > 0c>0): dimension (d+pp)\binom{d + p}{p}(pd+p​)
Gaussian (RBF)exp⁡(−γ∥x−z∥22)\exp(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{z}\rVert_2^2)exp(−γ∥x−z∥22​)infinite-dimensional (Section 9.3.3)

A kernel defines a geometry in the feature space without describing it. The squared norm of ϕ(x)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x})ϕ(x) is k(x,x)k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})k(x,x), and the squared distance between two images is ∥ϕ(x)−ϕ(z)∥2=k(x,x)+k(z,z)−2k(x,z)\lVert\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\rVert^2 = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}) + k(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}) - 2k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})∥ϕ(x)−ϕ(z)∥2=k(x,x)+k(z,z)−2k(x,z). For the Gaussian kernel k(x,x)=1k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}) = 1k(x,x)=1 for every x\mathbf{x}x: all the images lie on the unit sphere of the feature space, their squared distance is 2−2k(x,z)∈[0,2)2 - 2k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})\in[0, 2)2−2k(x,z)∈[0,2), and kkk is the cosine of the angle between them, a similarity that goes from 1 (the same point) to 0 (very far apart). The parameter γ\gammaγ is the inverse of the squared length scale: k=e−1k = e^{-1}k=e−1 at the distance 1/γ1/\sqrt\gamma1/γ​.

x_we = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])                                           # constructed example
y_we = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 2.0])
K_we = np.minimum.outer(x_we, x_we)

print("sklearn KernelRidge, dual coefficients:", krr_we.dual_coef_.round(10))
new_x = np.array([0.5, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 4.0])
print("prediction at", new_x, "=", (np.minimum.outer(new_x, x_we) @ alpha_we).round(10), "  (= min(2, x))")

9.3 Which functions are kernels?¶

9.3.1 A characterization¶

Given a candidate function kkk, how do we know that there is a feature map behind it? The answer is a property of the matrices K\mathbf{K}K that kkk produces.

Theorem 9.1 (characterization of kernels)

A symmetric function k:X×X→Rk:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}k:X×X→R is a kernel if and only if, for every finite set of points x1,…,xm\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_mx1​,…,xm​ of X\mathcal{X}X, its Gram matrix is positive semidefinite:

∑i,j=1mcicj k(xi,xj) ≥ 0for all c∈Rm.\sum_{i,j=1}^mc_ic_j\,k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)\ \ge\ 0\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^m.i,j=1∑m​ci​cj​k(xi​,xj​) ≥ 0for all c∈Rm.
(3)

(Such a function is also called a positive semidefinite kernel.)

Proof

A kernel has positive semidefinite Gram matrices. If k(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) = \langle\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\ranglek(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩ then ∑i,jcicjk(xi,xj)=⟨∑iciϕ(xi),∑jcjϕ(xj)⟩=∥∑iciϕ(xi)∥2≥0\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) = \big\langle\sum_ic_i\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i), \sum_jc_j\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_j)\big\rangle = \big\lVert\sum_ic_i\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\big\rVert^2\ge 0∑i,j​ci​cj​k(xi​,xj​)=⟨∑i​ci​ϕ(xi​),∑j​cj​ϕ(xj​)⟩=∥∥​∑i​ci​ϕ(xi​)∥∥​2≥0. Conversely, positive semidefinite Gram matrices give a feature map. For a finite set of points the construction is immediate: a symmetric positive semidefinite K=UΛU⊤\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{U}^\topK=UΛU⊤ has the square root Λ1/2U⊤\boldsymbol\Lambda^{1/2}\mathbf{U}^\topΛ1/2U⊤, whose columns ϕi=Λ1/2U⊤ei∈Rm\boldsymbol\phi_i = \boldsymbol\Lambda^{1/2}\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{e}_i\in\mathbb{R}^mϕi​=Λ1/2U⊤ei​∈Rm satisfy ϕi⊤ϕj=Kij\boldsymbol\phi_i^\top\boldsymbol\phi_j = K_{ij}ϕi⊤​ϕj​=Kij​. For the whole of X\mathcal{X}X one builds the feature space directly from kkk: it is the space of functions spanned by the k(⋅,x)k(\cdot, \mathbf{x})k(⋅,x) with the inner product ⟨k(⋅,x),k(⋅,z)⟩=k(x,z)\langle k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}), k(\cdot, \mathbf{z})\rangle = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})⟨k(⋅,x),k(⋅,z)⟩=k(x,z), the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of Section 9.4 (the condition is exactly what makes this inner product positive), and ϕ(x)=k(⋅,x)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}) = k(\cdot, \mathbf{x})ϕ(x)=k(⋅,x) (Moore–Aronszajn theorem). □\square□

The first half of the proof shows what is going on: a Gram matrix is a matrix of inner products, and inner products make positive semidefinite matrices. It also gives a practical test: a function is not a kernel as soon as one Gram matrix has a negative eigenvalue. The test can only refute (it cannot prove that a function is a kernel, which needs the algebra of the next section), but it is a useful sanity check for a kernel that we have made up. The rank of the Gram matrix has an interpretation too: it cannot exceed the dimension of the feature space. We compute the Gram matrices of the 150 Iris flowers (standardized) for the kernels of the table and for three functions that are not kernels: the sigmoid function tanh⁡(γ x⊤z+c)\tanh(\gamma\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + c)tanh(γx⊤z+c), which was used in early neural-network-inspired SVMs, the negative squared distance, and the distance itself.

iris = load_iris()
X_iris = StandardScaler().fit_transform(iris.data)
candidates = {
    "linear  x.z": linear_kernel(X_iris),
    "polynomial (x.z + 1)^3": polynomial_kernel(X_iris, degree=3, gamma=1, coef0=1),
    "Gaussian exp(-0.5 |x-z|^2)": rbf_kernel(X_iris, gamma=0.5),
    "Laplacian exp(-0.5 |x-z|_1)": laplacian_kernel(X_iris, gamma=0.5),
    "sigmoid tanh(0.5 x.z - 1)": sigmoid_kernel(X_iris, gamma=0.5, coef0=-1),
    "sigmoid tanh(x.z)": sigmoid_kernel(X_iris, gamma=1, coef0=0),
    "minus squared distance": -np.sum((X_iris[:, None, :] - X_iris[None, :, :]) ** 2, axis=2),
    "distance |x-z|": np.linalg.norm(X_iris[:, None, :] - X_iris[None, :, :], axis=2),
}
rows = []
for name, K_ in candidates.items():
    ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh((K_ + K_.T) / 2)
    rows.append({"function": name, "smallest eigenvalue": ev.min(), "largest eigenvalue": ev.max(),
                 "negative eigenvalues": int(np.sum(ev < -1e-10 * ev.max())), "rank": int(np.sum(ev > 1e-10 * ev.max()))})
print(f"{X_iris.shape[0]} flowers, {X_iris.shape[1]} features")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3e}"))

Laplacian exp(-0.5 |x-z|_1)           -9.484e-17           3.337e+01                     0   149

The kernels of the table pass the test: the smallest eigenvalue is at the level of the rounding errors (∣λmin⁡∣≤3⋅10−12\lvert\lambda_{\min}\rvert\le 3\cdot 10^{-12}∣λmin​∣≤3⋅10−12, against largest eigenvalues between 33 and 1.5⋅1041.5\cdot 10^41.5⋅104). The ranks read as the dimensions of the feature spaces: 4 for the linear kernel, 35=(4+33)35 = \binom{4 + 3}{3}35=(34+3​) for the polynomial kernel of degree 3, and 149 for the Gaussian and the Laplacian kernels, which is the number of distinct flowers (the data set contains one repeated measurement): their feature spaces are infinite-dimensional, so that the images of any distinct points are linearly independent. The three other functions are not kernels, and the test shows it: tanh⁡(0.5 x⊤z−1)\tanh(0.5\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} - 1)tanh(0.5x⊤z−1) has 73 negative eigenvalues (the smallest is -73, against a largest of 88) and tanh⁡(x⊤z)\tanh(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z})tanh(x⊤z) has 74, the negative squared distance has one, and the distance ∥x−z∥\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{z}\rVert∥x−z∥ has 148. For such a function there is no feature space behind it, and the dual problem of the SVM is no longer a concave maximization: it may have several local solutions or be unbounded. Software will still run (scikit-learn accepts the sigmoid kernel), but the guarantees of Chapter 8 are lost.

9.3.2 Building kernels from kernels¶

A few operations produce kernels from kernels, and they are enough to prove that all the kernels of the table are legitimate.

Proposition 9.2 (closure properties)

Let k1,k2k_1, k_2k1​,k2​ be kernels, a≥0a\ge 0a≥0 and g:X→Rg:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}g:X→R any function. Then the following are kernels: (i) k1+k2k_1 + k_2k1​+k2​ and a k1a\,k_1ak1​; (ii) the product k1k2k_1k_2k1​k2​; (iii) g(x) k1(x,z) g(z)g(\mathbf{x})\,k_1(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})\,g(\mathbf{z})g(x)k1​(x,z)g(z); (iv) q(k1(x,z))q\big(k_1(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})\big)q(k1​(x,z)) for a polynomial qqq with non-negative coefficients; (v) exp⁡(k1(x,z))\exp\big(k_1(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})\big)exp(k1​(x,z)); (vi) the pointwise limit of a sequence of kernels.

Proof

Let ϕ1,ϕ2\boldsymbol\phi_1, \boldsymbol\phi_2ϕ1​,ϕ2​ be feature maps of k1,k2k_1, k_2k1​,k2​. (i) The concatenated map (ϕ1,ϕ2)(\boldsymbol\phi_1, \boldsymbol\phi_2)(ϕ1​,ϕ2​) has the inner product k1+k2k_1 + k_2k1​+k2​, and a ϕ1\sqrt a\,\boldsymbol\phi_1a​ϕ1​ the inner product a k1a\,k_1ak1​. (ii) The tensor product ϕ1(x)⊗ϕ2(x)\boldsymbol\phi_1(\mathbf{x})\otimes\boldsymbol\phi_2(\mathbf{x})ϕ1​(x)⊗ϕ2​(x) (the vector of all the products ϕ1,r(x)ϕ2,s(x)\phi_{1,r}(\mathbf{x})\phi_{2,s}(\mathbf{x})ϕ1,r​(x)ϕ2,s​(x)) has the inner product ∑r,sϕ1,r(x)ϕ2,s(x)ϕ1,r(z)ϕ2,s(z)=k1(x,z)k2(x,z)\sum_{r,s}\phi_{1,r}(\mathbf{x})\phi_{2,s}(\mathbf{x})\phi_{1,r}(\mathbf{z})\phi_{2,s}(\mathbf{z}) = k_1(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})k_2(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})∑r,s​ϕ1,r​(x)ϕ2,s​(x)ϕ1,r​(z)ϕ2,s​(z)=k1​(x,z)k2​(x,z). In matrix terms this is the Schur product theorem: the entrywise product of two positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite. (iii) g(x)ϕ1(x)g(\mathbf{x})\boldsymbol\phi_1(\mathbf{x})g(x)ϕ1​(x) is a feature map. (iv) follows from (i), (ii) and the fact that a constant a≥0a\ge 0a≥0 is a kernel (the feature map a\sqrt aa​). (v) exp⁡(k1)=∑m≥0k1m/m!\exp(k_1) = \sum_{m\ge 0}k_1^m/m!exp(k1​)=∑m≥0​k1m​/m! is a limit of polynomials with non-negative coefficients, a pointwise limit of kernels by (iv), and (vi) holds because the set of positive semidefinite matrices is closed. □\square□

Applying the proposition: the polynomial kernel (γ x⊤z+c)p(\gamma\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + c)^p(γx⊤z+c)p is a kernel by (iv), since x⊤z\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z}x⊤z is one and γ,c≥0\gamma, c\ge 0γ,c≥0 (its feature space has dimension (d+pp)\binom{d+p}{p}(pd+p​) for c>0c > 0c>0: for d=4d = 4d=4 and p=3p = 3p=3 the rank 35 of the Gram matrix above). For the Gaussian kernel write

exp⁡(−γ∥x−z∥2)=e−γ∥x∥2 exp⁡(2γ x⊤z) e−γ∥z∥2:\exp\big(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{z}\rVert^2\big) = e^{-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert^2}\ \exp\big(2\gamma\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z}\big)\ e^{-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{z}\rVert^2}:exp(−γ∥x−z∥2)=e−γ∥x∥2 exp(2γx⊤z) e−γ∥z∥2:
(4)

the middle factor is a kernel by (v), the outer factors are the function ggg of (iii), so it is a kernel. (Section 9.3.3 shows the feature map.) The sigmoid kernel is not in the list, and indeed the table above shows that it has many negative eigenvalues on real data.

9.3.3 The Gaussian kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature space¶

The expansion of the exponential gives the feature map explicitly. In one dimension, exp⁡(2γxz)=∑n≥0(2γ)nn!xnzn\exp(2\gamma xz) = \sum_{n\ge 0}\frac{(2\gamma)^n}{n!}x^nz^nexp(2γxz)=∑n≥0​n!(2γ)n​xnzn, so that

ϕ(x)=(e−γx2(2γ)nn! xn)n=0,1,2,… ∈ R∞,e−γ(x−z)2=∑n=0∞ϕn(x)ϕn(z).\boldsymbol\phi(x) = \Big(e^{-\gamma x^2}\sqrt{\tfrac{(2\gamma)^n}{n!}}\,x^n\Big)_{n = 0, 1, 2, \dots}\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{\infty}, \qquad e^{-\gamma(x - z)^2} = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty\phi_n(x)\phi_n(z).ϕ(x)=(e−γx2n!(2γ)n​​xn)n=0,1,2,…​ ∈ R∞,e−γ(x−z)2=n=0∑∞​ϕn​(x)ϕn​(z).
(5)

Each feature is a monomial damped by a Gaussian envelope, and there is one for every degree: a linear model in these features is a polynomial of infinite degree (damped at infinity), which is why a Gaussian-kernel classifier can have arbitrarily complicated boundaries. The cell truncates the sum after NNN terms and measures how well the first NNN features reproduce the kernel on a grid of points of [−2,2][-2, 2][−2,2] (with γ=12\gamma = \frac12γ=21​). The second ingredient of Figure 9.1 is the spectrum of the Gaussian Gram matrix on real data, the Breast Cancer training patients: since the images ϕ(xi)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)ϕ(xi​) of distinct points are linearly independent (Gaussian Gram matrices of distinct points are positive definite; Micchelli, 1986), the matrix has full rank, but its eigenvalues decay quickly, and the number of eigenvalues that are not negligible measures the effective dimension of the sample in the feature space.

gamma_1d = 0.5
grid_1d = np.linspace(-2, 2, 81)
K_exact_1d = np.exp(-gamma_1d * np.subtract.outer(grid_1d, grid_1d) ** 2)


def phi_gauss_1d(x, n_terms, gamma=gamma_1d):
    return np.column_stack([np.exp(-gamma * x**2) * np.sqrt((2 * gamma) ** n / factorial(n)) * x**n for n in range(n_terms)])


trunc_rows = []
for N in [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20]:
    F_ = phi_gauss_1d(grid_1d, N)
    trunc_rows.append({"N": N, "largest error": np.abs(F_ @ F_.T - K_exact_1d).max()})
trunc = pd.DataFrame(trunc_rows)
print("first N features of the Gaussian kernel (gamma = 1/2, points in [-2, 2]):")
print(trunc.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2e}"))

bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
Xb = bc.data.to_numpy()
yb = (1 - bc.target).to_numpy().astype(int)                                  # malignant = 1, as in Chapters 6 to 8
Xb_tr, Xb_te, yb_tr, yb_te = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=yb)
scaler_b = StandardScaler().fit(Xb_tr)
Zb, Zb_te = scaler_b.transform(Xb_tr), scaler_b.transform(Xb_te)
sb, sb_te = 2.0 * yb_tr - 1, 2.0 * yb_te - 1                                 # labels in {-1, +1}
n_b = len(sb)
spectra = {g: np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(rbf_kernel(Zb, gamma=g)))[::-1] for g in [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0]}
rows = [{"gamma": g, "largest eigenvalue": ev[0], "smallest eigenvalue": ev[-1], "eigenvalues > 1e-3 of the largest": int(np.sum(ev > 1e-3 * ev[0])),
         "eigenvalues > 1e-6 of the largest": int(np.sum(ev > 1e-6 * ev[0]))} for g, ev in spectra.items()]
print(f"\nGaussian Gram matrix of the {n_b} training patients of Breast Cancer:")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))

# Figure 9.1 — the feature space of the Gaussian kernel
def figure_9_1():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.2))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.semilogy(trunc["N"], trunc["largest error"], color=BLUE, lw=2, marker="o", ms=5)
    ax.set(xlabel="number of features $N$ kept", ylabel="largest error of $\\sum_{n<N}\\phi_n(x)\\phi_n(z)$", title="(a) one dimension: the explicit feature map")
    ax.set_xticks([1, 5, 10, 15, 20])
    ax = axes[1]
    for (g, ev), color, marker in zip(spectra.items(), [BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE, VERMILION], ["o", "s", "^", "D"]):
        idx = np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(0, np.log10(len(ev)), 40)).astype(int)) - 1
        ax.semilogy(idx + 1, np.maximum(ev[idx], 1e-16), color=color, marker=marker, ms=4, lw=1.6, label=f"$\\gamma = {g:g}$")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="index of the eigenvalue", ylabel="eigenvalue of the Gram matrix", title=f"(b) Breast Cancer: spectrum of the Gaussian Gram matrix", ylim=(1e-8, 1e3))
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_9_1()

Fifteen features reproduce the Gaussian kernel on [−2,2][-2, 2][−2,2] to 2⋅10−52\cdot 10^{-5}2⋅10−5 and twenty to 10-8: an infinite-dimensional feature map is effectively low-dimensional when the points live in a bounded region, because the damping makes the features of high degree negligible. Panel (b) says the same of real data. For γ=0.001\gamma = 0.001γ=0.001 only 8 of the 426 eigenvalues exceed 10-3 of the largest, and 98 exceed 10-6; for γ=0.01\gamma = 0.01γ=0.01, 48 and 358; for γ=0.1\gamma = 0.1γ=0.1, 381 and all 426; for γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 the matrix is close to the identity (its eigenvalues are between 0.64 and 1.76): the images of the 426 patients are nearly orthogonal. The parameter γ\gammaγ sets the effective dimension of the feature space seen by the sample, from a few smooth directions (almost linear functions) to nnn (every patient has a direction of its own: memorization, Section 9.6).

9.4 The representer theorem¶

9.4.1 The space of functions behind a kernel¶

So far a kernel has been a way to compute inner products. The second use is as a space of functions, in which the learning problem can be written and solved. Let kkk be a kernel. For each point x\mathbf{x}x, the function k(⋅,x):z↦k(z,x)k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}):\mathbf{z}\mapsto k(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})k(⋅,x):z↦k(z,x) is a function on X\mathcal{X}X (for the Gaussian kernel, a bump of width 1/γ1/\sqrt\gamma1/γ​ centered at x\mathbf{x}x). Consider the functions that are finite combinations of such bumps, f=∑i=1mai k(⋅,xi)f = \sum_{i=1}^ma_i\,k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i=1m​ai​k(⋅,xi​), with the inner product defined by bilinearity from ⟨k(⋅,x),k(⋅,z)⟩=k(x,z)\langle k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}), k(\cdot, \mathbf{z})\rangle = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})⟨k(⋅,x),k(⋅,z)⟩=k(x,z):

⟨∑iaik(⋅,xi), ∑jbjk(⋅,zj)⟩=∑i,jaibj k(xi,zj),∥∑iaik(⋅,xi)∥2=a⊤Ka ≥0.\Big\langle\sum_ia_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i),\ \sum_jb_jk(\cdot, \mathbf{z}_j)\Big\rangle = \sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\,k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{z}_j), \qquad \Big\lVert\sum_ia_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)\Big\rVert^2 = \mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{K}\mathbf{a}\ \ge 0 .⟨i∑​ai​k(⋅,xi​), j∑​bj​k(⋅,zj​)⟩=i,j∑​ai​bj​k(xi​,zj​),∥∥​i∑​ai​k(⋅,xi​)∥∥​2=a⊤Ka ≥0.
(6)

The positivity is exactly the property of Theorem 9.1, and completing the space of these functions with respect to the norm gives a Hilbert space Hk\mathcal{H}_kHk​ of functions on X\mathcal{X}X, the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of kkk. Its name comes from the identity that evaluating fff at a point is an inner product with a bump:

 f(x)=⟨f, k(⋅,x)⟩ (reproducing property),\boxed{\ f(\mathbf{x}) = \langle f,\ k(\cdot, \mathbf{x})\rangle\ }\qquad\text{(reproducing property)}, f(x)=⟨f, k(⋅,x)⟩ ​(reproducing property),
(7)

which for f=∑iaik(⋅,xi)f = \sum_ia_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i​ai​k(⋅,xi​) is ∑iaik(xi,x)\sum_ia_ik(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x})∑i​ai​k(xi​,x) by the definition of the inner product, and extends to the limits. Two consequences. First, ϕ(x)=k(⋅,x)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}) = k(\cdot, \mathbf{x})ϕ(x)=k(⋅,x) is a feature map of kkk (by the definition of the inner product, ⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩=k(x,z)\langle\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\rangle = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩=k(x,z)), the one that completes the proof of Theorem 9.1. Second, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, ∣f(x)∣≤∥f∥Hk(x,x)\lvert f(\mathbf{x})\rvert\le\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}\sqrt{k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})}∣f(x)∣≤∥f∥H​k(x,x)​: a function with a small norm is small everywhere, and two functions with close norms and close values on the data are close elsewhere. The norm ∥f∥H\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}∥f∥H​ is a measure of the complexity of fff, and the kernel decides which functions are simple. For the linear kernel Hk={x↦w⊤x}\mathcal{H}_k = \{\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}\}Hk​={x↦w⊤x} and ∥f∥H=∥w∥\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}} = \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥f∥H​=∥w∥, the norm that we have penalized since Chapter 6; for the Gaussian kernel ∥f∥H\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}∥f∥H​ penalizes high frequencies, with a weighting set by γ\gammaγ (the wider the bump, the more expensive the high frequencies, hence smooth functions are cheap).

9.4.2 The theorem¶

Theorem 9.4 (representer theorem; Kimeldorf and Wahba, 1971; Schölkopf, Herbrich and Smola, 2001)

Let kkk be a kernel with RKHS H\mathcal{H}H, (xi,yi)i≤n(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)_{i\le n}(xi​,yi​)i≤n​ a training set, LLL any function of the values f(x1),…,f(xn)f(\mathbf{x}_1), \dots, f(\mathbf{x}_n)f(x1​),…,f(xn​) (the loss on the sample, with any dependence on the labels), and Ω:[0,∞)→R\Omega:[0, \infty)\to\mathbb{R}Ω:[0,∞)→R non-decreasing. Then the problem

min⁡f∈H L(f(x1),…,f(xn))+Ω(∥f∥H)\min_{f\in\mathcal{H}}\ L\big(f(\mathbf{x}_1), \dots, f(\mathbf{x}_n)\big) + \Omega\big(\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}\big)f∈Hmin​ L(f(x1​),…,f(xn​))+Ω(∥f∥H​)
(8)

has a minimizer (if it has any) of the form f=∑i=1nαi k(⋅,xi)f = \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i=1n​αi​k(⋅,xi​). If Ω\OmegaΩ is strictly increasing, every minimizer has this form.

Proof

Let S=span⁡{k(⋅,x1),…,k(⋅,xn)}\mathcal{S} = \operatorname{span}\{k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_1), \dots, k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_n)\}S=span{k(⋅,x1​),…,k(⋅,xn​)}, a finite-dimensional, hence closed, subspace of H\mathcal{H}H. Every f∈Hf\in\mathcal{H}f∈H decomposes uniquely as f=f∥+f⊥f = f_\parallel + f_\perpf=f∥​+f⊥​ with f∥∈Sf_\parallel\in\mathcal{S}f∥​∈S and f⊥f_\perpf⊥​ orthogonal to S\mathcal{S}S. By the reproducing property, f(xi)=⟨f,k(⋅,xi)⟩=⟨f∥,k(⋅,xi)⟩+⟨f⊥,k(⋅,xi)⟩=f∥(xi)f(\mathbf{x}_i) = \langle f, k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)\rangle = \langle f_\parallel, k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)\rangle + \langle f_\perp, k(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)\rangle = f_\parallel(\mathbf{x}_i)f(xi​)=⟨f,k(⋅,xi​)⟩=⟨f∥​,k(⋅,xi​)⟩+⟨f⊥​,k(⋅,xi​)⟩=f∥​(xi​), because k(⋅,xi)∈Sk(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)\in\mathcal{S}k(⋅,xi​)∈S is orthogonal to f⊥f_\perpf⊥​. So fff and f∥f_\parallelf∥​ have the same values on the sample, and the same loss LLL. By the Pythagorean theorem ∥f∥2=∥f∥∥2+∥f⊥∥2≥∥f∥∥2\lVert f\rVert^2 = \lVert f_\parallel\rVert^2 + \lVert f_\perp\rVert^2\ge\lVert f_\parallel\rVert^2∥f∥2=∥f∥​∥2+∥f⊥​∥2≥∥f∥​∥2, hence Ω(∥f∥)≥Ω(∥f∥∥)\Omega(\lVert f\rVert)\ge\Omega(\lVert f_\parallel\rVert)Ω(∥f∥)≥Ω(∥f∥​∥): replacing fff by f∥f_\parallelf∥​ does not increase the objective, and a minimizer can be taken in S\mathcal{S}S. If Ω\OmegaΩ is strictly increasing and f⊥≠0f_\perp\ne 0f⊥​=0, the inequality is strict, so no minimizer can have f⊥≠0f_\perp\ne 0f⊥​=0. □\square□

The theorem is remarkable because the problem is posed in an infinite-dimensional space and the solution lives in an nnn-dimensional one. With f=∑iαik(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i\alpha_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i​αi​k(⋅,xi​) we have f(xj)=(Kα)jf(\mathbf{x}_j) = (\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha)_jf(xj​)=(Kα)j​ and ∥f∥H2=α⊤Kα\lVert f\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}} = \boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha∥f∥H2​=α⊤Kα, so the problem becomes

min⁡α∈Rn L(Kα)+Ω(α⊤Kα),\min_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ L(\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha) + \Omega\big(\sqrt{\boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha}\big),α∈Rnmin​ L(Kα)+Ω(α⊤Kα​),
(9)

which involves the data only through the Gram matrix. The methods that we know are instances:

  • Ridge regression (Chapter 6): L=∑i(yi−f(xi))2L = \sum_i(y_i - f(\mathbf{x}_i))^2L=∑i​(yi​−f(xi​))2, Ω=λ∥f∥2\Omega = \lambda\lVert f\rVert^2Ω=λ∥f∥2, linear kernel; the theorem says that w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ is a combination of the training points, Proposition 6.12.

  • The soft-margin SVM (Chapter 8): by Proposition 8.3 the problem is ∑imax⁡{0,1−yif(xi)}+λ2∥f∥2\sum_i\max\{0, 1 - y_if(\mathbf{x}_i)\} + \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert f\rVert^2∑i​max{0,1−yi​f(xi​)}+2λ​∥f∥2 (with the intercept separate); the theorem gives f=∑iαiyik(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i\alpha_iy_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i​αi​yi​k(⋅,xi​) a priori, which Theorem 8.4 derived by Lagrangian duality.

  • Kernel logistic regression: the same with the log-loss; every coefficient is non-zero (Section 8.4.1).

  • Support vector regression (Section 8.8.2): the ε\varepsilonε-insensitive loss.

The dual forms of Chapters 6 and 8 are not accidents of those problems: every penalized method with a norm penalty in a space of functions has one. (Without the strict monotonicity, or with a penalty that is not a function of the norm, such as the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm of Chapter 10, the theorem does not apply.)

9.4.3 Capacity: the margin bound in a feature space¶

The proof of Proposition 3.6 used only that the functions are inner products with a vector of norm at most BBB, so it applies in H\mathcal{H}H word for word, with ϕ(xi)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)ϕ(xi​) in the role of xi\mathbf{x}_ixi​.

Proposition 9.5 (Rademacher complexity of a ball of the RKHS)

Let FB={f∈H:∥f∥H≤B}\mathcal{F}_B = \{f\in\mathcal{H} : \lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}\le B\}FB​={f∈H:∥f∥H​≤B}. The empirical Rademacher complexity on the sample x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​ satisfies

R^S(FB) ≤ Bn∑i=1nk(xi,xi) ≤ BRn,R=sup⁡xk(x,x).\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}_B)\ \le\ \frac{B}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^nk(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_i)}\ \le\ \frac{BR}{\sqrt n},\qquad R = \sup_{\mathbf{x}}\sqrt{k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})}.R^S​(FB​) ≤ nB​i=1∑n​k(xi​,xi​)​ ≤ n​BR​,R=xsup​k(x,x)​.
(10)

Consequently, Theorem 3.7 holds for the kernel classifiers sign⁡f(x)\operatorname{sign} f(\mathbf{x})signf(x), f∈FBf\in\mathcal{F}_Bf∈FB​, with B=∥f∥HB = \lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}B=∥f∥H​ and RRR the radius of the images, sup⁡x∥ϕ(x)∥\sup_{\mathbf{x}}\lVert\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x})\rVertsupx​∥ϕ(x)∥.

Proof. With Rademacher signs σi\sigma_iσi​, ∑iσif(xi)=⟨f,∑iσiϕ(xi)⟩≤B∥∑iσiϕ(xi)∥\sum_i\sigma_if(\mathbf{x}_i) = \langle f, \sum_i\sigma_i\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rangle\le B\big\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\big\rVert∑i​σi​f(xi​)=⟨f,∑i​σi​ϕ(xi​)⟩≤B∥∥​∑i​σi​ϕ(xi​)∥∥​ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and by Jensen’s inequality E∥∑iσiϕ(xi)∥≤E∥∑iσiϕ(xi)∥2=∑i∥ϕ(xi)∥2=∑ik(xi,xi)\mathbb{E}\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rVert\le\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rVert^2} = \sqrt{\sum_i\lVert\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)\rVert^2} = \sqrt{\sum_ik(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_i)}E∥∑i​σi​ϕ(xi​)∥≤E∥∑i​σi​ϕ(xi​)∥2​=∑i​∥ϕ(xi​)∥2​=∑i​k(xi​,xi​)​, since the cross terms have zero mean. □\square□

The capacity of a kernel classifier does not depend on the dimension of the feature space (infinite for the Gaussian kernel) but only on ∥f∥H\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}∥f∥H​ and on RRR. For the Gaussian kernel R=1R = 1R=1, whatever γ\gammaγ and the data: no outlier inflates the radius, which was the problem with the bound of Section 8.6.1 for the linear kernel. This is the reconciliation with Chapter 3: the class of all functions of the RKHS has an infinite VC dimension (Section 9.3.3: any labeling of distinct points can be interpolated), but the balls FB\mathcal{F}_BFB​ have a finite Rademacher complexity, and the regularization parameter chooses BBB. Section 9.6.3 evaluates the bound on a real data set.

9.5 Kernel ridge regression¶

9.5.1 The solution, and what it does¶

Take the squared loss and the penalty λ∥f∥H2\lambda\lVert f\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}}λ∥f∥H2​. The response is centered (we subtract the mean of the training responses and add it back to the predictions), as in Lemma 6.3, so that no intercept is needed. By Theorem 9.4 we look for f=∑iαik(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i\alpha_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i​αi​k(⋅,xi​) and minimize ∥y−Kα∥2+λα⊤Kα\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha\rVert^2 + \lambda\boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha∥y−Kα∥2+λα⊤Kα.

Proposition 9.6 (kernel ridge regression)

For λ>0\lambda > 0λ>0 the problem min⁡f∈H∑i(yi−f(xi))2+λ∥f∥H2\min_{f\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_i(y_i - f(\mathbf{x}_i))^2 + \lambda\lVert f\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}}minf∈H​∑i​(yi​−f(xi​))2+λ∥f∥H2​ has the unique solution f^=∑iα^ik(⋅,xi)\hat f = \sum_i\hat\alpha_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f^​=∑i​α^i​k(⋅,xi​) with

α^=(K+λIn)−1y,y^=Kα^=Hλy,Hλ=K(K+λI)−1.\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I}_n)^{-1}\mathbf{y}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{K}\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} = \mathbf{H}_\lambda\mathbf{y},\quad\mathbf{H}_\lambda = \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}.α^=(K+λIn​)−1y,y^​=Kα^=Hλ​y,Hλ​=K(K+λI)−1.
(11)

(i) For the linear kernel it is the ridge regression of Chapter 6. (ii) If K=Udiag⁡(μ1,…,μn)U⊤\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{U}\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n)\mathbf{U}^\topK=Udiag(μ1​,…,μn​)U⊤ then y^=∑jμjμj+λ(uj⊤y) uj\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \sum_j\frac{\mu_j}{\mu_j + \lambda}(\mathbf{u}_j^\top\mathbf{y})\,\mathbf{u}_jy^​=∑j​μj​+λμj​​(uj⊤​y)uj​ and df⁡(λ)=tr⁡Hλ=∑jμjμj+λ\operatorname{df}(\lambda) = \operatorname{tr}\mathbf{H}_\lambda = \sum_j\frac{\mu_j}{\mu_j + \lambda}df(λ)=trHλ​=∑j​μj​+λμj​​. (iii) (leave-one-out) The prediction at xi\mathbf{x}_ixi​ of the model fitted without example iii, with the same λ\lambdaλ, has the error yi−y^i1−(Hλ)ii\dfrac{y_i - \hat y_i}{1 - (\mathbf{H}_\lambda)_{ii}}1−(Hλ​)ii​yi​−y^​i​​.

Proof

Solution. The objective is J(α)=∥y−Kα∥2+λα⊤KαJ(\boldsymbol\alpha) = \lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha\rVert^2 + \lambda\boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alphaJ(α)=∥y−Kα∥2+λα⊤Kα, with gradient −2K(y−Kα)+2λKα=2K[(K+λI)α−y]-2\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha) + 2\lambda\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha = 2\mathbf{K}\big[(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol\alpha - \mathbf{y}\big]−2K(y−Kα)+2λKα=2K[(K+λI)α−y], which vanishes at α^=(K+λI)−1y\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y}α^=(K+λI)−1y (K+λI\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I}K+λI is positive definite). JJJ is convex, so this is a minimizer, and the function f^\hat ff^​ is unique by the strict monotonicity of Ω(t)=λt2\Omega(t) = \lambda t^2Ω(t)=λt2 in Theorem 9.4 and the strict convexity of the problem in Kα\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alphaKα. (i) With K=XX⊤\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\topK=XX⊤ this is the dual form of Proposition 6.12. (ii) Hλ\mathbf{H}_\lambdaHλ​ and K\mathbf{K}K have the same eigenvectors, with eigenvalues μj/(μj+λ)\mu_j/(\mu_j + \lambda)μj​/(μj​+λ). (iii) Let f^(−i)\hat f^{(-i)}f^​(−i) be the solution without example iii. Consider the full problem with yiy_iyi​ replaced by y~i=f^(−i)(xi)\tilde y_i = \hat f^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i)y~​i​=f^​(−i)(xi​). For this modified data set, f^(−i)\hat f^{(-i)}f^​(−i) is still a minimizer: it minimizes the objective of the reduced problem, and the extra term (y~i−f(xi))2≥0(\tilde y_i - f(\mathbf{x}_i))^2\ge 0(y~​i​−f(xi​))2≥0 vanishes at f=f^(−i)f = \hat f^{(-i)}f=f^​(−i). By uniqueness the fit of the modified problem is f^(−i)\hat f^{(-i)}f^​(−i), and since the fit is linear in the responses, f^(−i)(xi)=∑j≠i(Hλ)ijyj+(Hλ)iif^(−i)(xi)\hat f^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i) = \sum_{j\ne i}(\mathbf{H}_\lambda)_{ij}y_j + (\mathbf{H}_\lambda)_{ii}\hat f^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i)f^​(−i)(xi​)=∑j=i​(Hλ​)ij​yj​+(Hλ​)ii​f^​(−i)(xi​). Solving, f^(−i)(xi)=(y^i−(Hλ)iiyi)/(1−(Hλ)ii)\hat f^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i) = (\hat y_i - (\mathbf{H}_\lambda)_{ii}y_i)/(1 - (\mathbf{H}_\lambda)_{ii})f^​(−i)(xi​)=(y^​i​−(Hλ​)ii​yi​)/(1−(Hλ​)ii​), so yi−f^(−i)(xi)=(yi−y^i)/(1−(Hλ)ii)y_i - \hat f^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i) = (y_i - \hat y_i)/(1 - (\mathbf{H}_\lambda)_{ii})yi​−f^​(−i)(xi​)=(yi​−y^​i​)/(1−(Hλ​)ii​). □\square□

Part (ii) is the singular-value view of Section 6.3.2, transported to the Gram matrix: the eigenvectors of K\mathbf{K}K with large eigenvalues (smooth functions of the data) are kept, and those with small eigenvalues (oscillating functions) are shrunk by μj/(μj+λ)\mu_j/(\mu_j + \lambda)μj​/(μj​+λ). Panel (b) of Figure 9.1 therefore shows what the Gaussian kernel can fit: for γ=0.001\gamma = 0.001γ=0.001 only a handful of directions have eigenvalues larger than a reasonable λ\lambdaλ, and the model is nearly linear. Part (iii) is Proposition 6.8 for the kernel, and it makes the choice of (γ,λ)(\gamma, \lambda)(γ,λ) cheap: one eigendecomposition per γ\gammaγ gives the leave-one-out error of every λ\lambdaλ, with no refit. The model with the response centered by its mean keeps the mean fixed in the leave-one-out computation, which is a very small simplification (Section 6.3.4 dealt with it in the same way).

A word about Exercise 4.8, the Nadaraya–Watson estimator f^h(x)=∑ik(x,xi)yi/∑ik(x,xi)\hat f_h(x) = \sum_ik(x, x_i)y_i/\sum_ik(x, x_i)f^​h​(x)=∑i​k(x,xi​)yi​/∑i​k(x,xi​) of Chapter 4: it is also a combination of kernel bumps centered at the training points, but its weights are fixed by the kernel, with no linear system to solve. It is the limiting case of kernel ridge regression in the memorization regime: when γ→∞\gamma\to\inftyγ→∞, K→I\mathbf{K}\to\mathbf{I}K→I and α^→y/(1+λ)\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}\to\mathbf{y}/(1 + \lambda)α^→y/(1+λ), so f^(x)→11+λ∑ik(x,xi)yi\hat f(x)\to\frac1{1 + \lambda}\sum_ik(x, x_i)y_if^​(x)→1+λ1​∑i​k(x,xi​)yi​, the numerator of the Nadaraya–Watson estimator without its normalization (a Parzen-window sum). Kernel ridge regression goes further: the matrix (K+λI)−1(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}(K+λI)−1 discounts the redundancy between neighboring bumps, which is what makes it a good smoother with a wide kernel (small γ\gammaγ) where the local average of Chapter 4 would be too crude.

9.5.2 Checks, and a regression experiment¶

The cell implements kernel ridge regression from scratch and checks three claims on the Diabetes data (331 training and 111 test patients, standardized features, the split of Chapters 6 and 7): that with the linear kernel it is the Ridge of scikit-learn (to machine precision), that the leave-one-out formula agrees with 331 explicit refits, and that the polynomial kernel (x⊤z+1)2(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + 1)^2(x⊤z+1)2 gives the same predictions as ridge regression on the explicit features, in the case of the two features bmi and s5 (six features), with the same coefficients w=Φ⊤α^\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol\Phi^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}w=Φ⊤α^ (the representer theorem in the finite-dimensional case).

diab = load_diabetes()
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(diab.data, diab.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED)
scaler_d = StandardScaler().fit(Xd_tr)
Zd, Zd_te = scaler_d.transform(Xd_tr), scaler_d.transform(Xd_te)
n_d = len(yd_tr)
y_mean = yd_tr.mean()
yc_d = yd_tr - y_mean                                                      # centered response


def krr_alpha(K, y, lam):
    """Dual coefficients (K + lam I)^{-1} y of kernel ridge regression."""
    return np.linalg.solve(K + lam * np.eye(len(y)), y)


def rmse(pred, y):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((pred - y) ** 2)))


# (1) linear kernel = ridge regression of Chapter 6
lam = 10.0
alpha_lin = krr_alpha(Zd @ Zd.T, yc_d, lam)
pred_krr = Zd_te @ Zd.T @ alpha_lin + y_mean
pred_ridge = Ridge(alpha=lam).fit(Zd, yd_tr).predict(Zd_te)
print(f"(1) linear kernel against Ridge(alpha={lam:g}): largest difference of the test predictions {np.abs(pred_krr - pred_ridge).max():.1e}")

# (2) leave-one-out shortcut against 331 refits (RBF kernel)
K_rbf = rbf_kernel(Zd, gamma=0.02)
lam = 1.0
H = K_rbf @ np.linalg.inv(K_rbf + lam * np.eye(n_d))
loo_shortcut = (yc_d - H @ yc_d) / (1 - np.diag(H))
loo_refit = np.empty(n_d)
for i in range(n_d):
    keep = np.delete(np.arange(n_d), i)
    loo_refit[i] = yc_d[i] - K_rbf[i, keep] @ krr_alpha(K_rbf[np.ix_(keep, keep)], yc_d[keep], lam)
print(f"(2) leave-one-out errors, shortcut against {n_d} refits: largest difference {np.abs(loo_shortcut - loo_refit).max():.1e}; "
      f"LOO RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean(loo_shortcut**2)):.2f}; effective degrees of freedom tr(H) = {np.trace(H):.1f}")

# (3) polynomial kernel against ridge on the explicit features, two features of Diabetes
cols = [list(diab.feature_names).index(c) for c in ["bmi", "s5"]]
P_tr, P_te = Zd[:, cols], Zd_te[:, cols]


def phi_poly2(X):
    x1, x2, r = X[:, 0], X[:, 1], np.sqrt(2)
    return np.c_[x1**2, x2**2, r * x1 * x2, r * x1, r * x2, np.ones(len(X))]


lam = 5.0
alpha_poly = krr_alpha((P_tr @ P_tr.T + 1) ** 2, yc_d, lam)                  # kernel (x.z + 1)^2
pred_kernel = ((P_te @ P_tr.T + 1) ** 2) @ alpha_poly + y_mean
F_tr, F_te = phi_poly2(P_tr), phi_poly2(P_te)
w_primal = np.linalg.solve(F_tr.T @ F_tr + lam * np.eye(6), F_tr.T @ yc_d)   # ridge on the 6 explicit features
print(f"(3) kernel (x.z + 1)^2 against ridge on 6 explicit features: predictions differ by {np.abs(pred_kernel - (F_te @ w_primal + y_mean)).max():.1e}; "
      f"w - Phi' alpha: {np.abs(w_primal - F_tr.T @ alpha_poly).max():.1e}; ||f||^2 = alpha' K alpha = {alpha_poly @ ((P_tr @ P_tr.T + 1) ** 2) @ alpha_poly:.3f} = ||w||^2 = {w_primal @ w_primal:.3f}")
(1) linear kernel against Ridge(alpha=10): largest difference of the test predictions 3.4e-13

(2) leave-one-out errors, shortcut against 331 refits: largest difference 1.2e-12; LOO RMSE 55.54; effective degrees of freedom tr(H) = 19.1
(3) kernel (x.z + 1)^2 against ridge on 6 explicit features: predictions differ by 3.5e-12; w - Phi' alpha: 2.7e-13; ||f||^2 = alpha' K alpha = 887.714 = ||w||^2 = 887.714

Now a regression experiment. For each γ\gammaγ of a grid and each λ\lambdaλ we compute the leave-one-out RMSE with the shortcut (one eigendecomposition per γ\gammaγ), choose the best pair, and measure the test RMSE once. The linear kernel (that is, ridge regression, with its own grid of λ\lambdaλ) is the benchmark.

def loo_grid(K, yc, lams):
    """Leave-one-out RMSE of kernel ridge regression for many lambdas from one eigendecomposition (Proposition 9.6)."""
    mu, U = np.linalg.eigh(K)
    uy = U.T @ yc
    out = []
    for lam in lams:
        shrink = mu / (mu + lam)
        resid = yc - U @ (shrink * uy)
        h = (U**2) @ shrink
        out.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((resid / (1 - h)) ** 2)))
    return np.array(out)


lams = 10.0 ** np.arange(-3, 4, 0.5)
gammas = [0.0003, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1]
rows = []
K_lin = Zd @ Zd.T
loo_lin = loo_grid(K_lin, yc_d, lams)
j = int(np.argmin(loo_lin))
alpha_ = krr_alpha(K_lin, yc_d, lams[j])
rows.append({"kernel": "linear (ridge)", "gamma": np.nan, "lambda": lams[j], "LOO RMSE": loo_lin[j], "test RMSE": rmse(Zd_te @ Zd.T @ alpha_ + y_mean, yd_te),
             "df": np.sum(np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_lin) / (np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_lin) + lams[j]))})
best = None
for g in gammas:
    K_ = rbf_kernel(Zd, gamma=g)
    loo_ = loo_grid(K_, yc_d, lams)
    j = int(np.argmin(loo_))
    mu_ = np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_)
    alpha_ = krr_alpha(K_, yc_d, lams[j])
    row = {"kernel": "Gaussian", "gamma": g, "lambda": lams[j], "LOO RMSE": loo_[j], "test RMSE": rmse(rbf_kernel(Zd_te, Zd, gamma=g) @ alpha_ + y_mean, yd_te),
           "df": np.sum(mu_ / (mu_ + lams[j]))}
    rows.append(row)
kr_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"{n_d} training patients; best LOO RMSE of each kernel over the grid of lambda")
print(kr_table.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))
print(f"RMSE of the baseline that predicts the training mean: {rmse(y_mean, yd_te):.2f}")
331 training patients; best LOO RMSE of each kernel over the grid of lambda
        kernel  gamma  lambda  LOO RMSE  test RMSE    df
linear (ridge)    NaN       1      55.5      53.32 9.688
      Gaussian 0.0003   0.001     55.53      52.42 14.58
      Gaussian  0.001    0.01     55.56      52.37 14.47
      Gaussian  0.003     0.1     55.52      52.31 13.28
      Gaussian   0.01  0.3162     55.51      51.66 18.72
      Gaussian   0.03       1     55.82      51.13 25.86
      Gaussian    0.1   3.162     57.81      51.58 35.05

The three checks hold to machine precision: kernel ridge regression with the linear kernel is Ridge (5⋅10−135\cdot 10^{-13}5⋅10−13); the leave-one-out shortcut matches 331 refits (10-12; for the Gaussian kernel with γ=0.02\gamma = 0.02γ=0.02 and λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 the leave-one-out RMSE is 55.5, with tr⁡Hλ=19.1\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{H}_\lambda = 19.1trHλ​=19.1 effective degrees of freedom); and the polynomial kernel (x⊤z+1)2(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + 1)^2(x⊤z+1)2 produces the predictions of ridge regression on the six explicit features (2⋅10−122\cdot 10^{-12}2⋅10−12), with w=Φ⊤α^\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol\Phi^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}w=Φ⊤α^ (5⋅10−135\cdot 10^{-13}5⋅10−13) and ∥f∥H2=α^⊤Kα^=∥w∥2=887.7\lVert f\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}} = \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}^\top\mathbf{K}\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} = \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = 887.7∥f∥H2​=α^⊤Kα^=∥w∥2=887.7. In the experiment, the leave-one-out RMSE of the Gaussian kernel is the same as that of ridge regression for every γ\gammaγ from 3⋅10−43\cdot 10^{-4}3⋅10−4 to 0.01 (55.5 against 55.5), and worse for the larger ones (55.8 at γ=0.03\gamma = 0.03γ=0.03, 57.8 at 0.1): for small γ\gammaγ the Gaussian kernel is nearly linear (Figure 9.1(b)), and for the larger ones it overfits. The test RMSE of the Gaussian models selected by the leave-one-out error is between 51.7 and 52.4, against 53.3 for ridge, a difference of one to one and a half points of RMSE that the leave-one-out error does not see, and that 111 test patients cannot confirm. The conclusion is the one of Section 6.7: on this data set a nonlinear kernel is not clearly better than a linear model, in spite of its larger effective number of parameters (13 to 19 degrees of freedom, against 9.7 for ridge). The baseline that predicts the mean has an RMSE of 74.9.

9.5.3 The effect of the two parameters on a real regression curve¶

To see what γ\gammaγ and λ\lambdaλ do we fit a single feature, the serum triglycerides s5 (on a log scale, standardized), against the disease progression of the 331 training patients. We keep the penalty λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 and vary the bandwidth: a small γ\gammaγ gives a nearly linear curve, a moderate γ\gammaγ a smooth curve with some curvature, and a large γ\gammaγ a curve that follows the noise, with a leave-one-out RMSE that shows it.

j_s5 = list(diab.feature_names).index("s5")
x_s5 = Zd[:, [j_s5]]
grid_s5 = np.linspace(x_s5.min() - 0.1, x_s5.max() + 0.1, 300)[:, None]
panels = []
for g, lam in [(0.05, 1.0), (1.0, 1.0), (30.0, 1.0)]:
    K_ = rbf_kernel(x_s5, gamma=g)
    alpha_ = krr_alpha(K_, yc_d, lam)
    mu_ = np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_)
    fit_ = rbf_kernel(grid_s5, x_s5, gamma=g) @ alpha_ + y_mean
    panels.append({"gamma": g, "lambda": lam, "fit": fit_, "df": np.sum(mu_ / (mu_ + lam)), "loo": loo_grid(K_, yc_d, [lam])[0],
                   "train": rmse(K_ @ alpha_ + y_mean, yd_tr)})
print(pd.DataFrame([{k: v for k, v in p.items() if k != "fit"} for p in panels]).rename(columns={"df": "effective df", "loo": "LOO RMSE", "train": "training RMSE"}).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2f}"))
 gamma  lambda  effective df  LOO RMSE  training RMSE
  0.05    1.00          2.78     65.45          64.95
  1.00    1.00          7.46     65.89          64.55
 30.00    1.00         26.58     66.89          61.84

# Figure 9.2 — kernel ridge regression of the disease progression on one feature, for three bandwidths
def figure_9_2():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.6, 3.9), sharey=True)
    for ax, p in zip(axes, panels):
        ax.scatter(x_s5[:, 0], yd_tr, s=12, color=SKY, alpha=0.8)
        ax.plot(grid_s5[:, 0], p["fit"], color="k", lw=2.2)
        ax.set(xlabel="log serum triglycerides (standardized)", title=f"$\\gamma = {p['gamma']:g}$: df $= {p['df']:.0f}$, LOO RMSE $= {p['loo']:.1f}$")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("disease progression")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_9_2()

With γ=0.05\gamma = 0.05γ=0.05 the curve is almost a straight line (about 3 effective degrees of freedom, besides the mean). With γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 it bends (7.5 degrees of freedom) and flattens at high values, but also turns upward at the left edge, where there are very few patients and the data cannot support it; the leave-one-out RMSE is a little worse than that of the nearly linear curve (65.9 against 65.5). With γ=30\gamma = 30γ=30 the curve follows the noise (26.6 degrees of freedom): its training RMSE is the lowest of the three (61.8 against 64.6 and 65.0) and its leave-one-out RMSE the highest (66.9), the signature of overfitting. One feature explains little of the disease progression (all three RMSE are close to 65, against the standard deviation of the response, 77.7), but the lesson on the roles of the parameters is general: γ\gammaγ and λ\lambdaλ both control the effective number of parameters, and so do the two together; they trade against one another (a larger λ\lambdaλ can compensate for a larger γ\gammaγ), which is why they must be chosen jointly.

9.6 Kernel support vector machines¶

9.6.1 The SMO of Chapter 8, unchanged¶

The function smo of Section 8.5.2 takes a Gram matrix, and nothing in it depends on how the matrix was computed: giving it the Gaussian Gram matrix instead of XX⊤\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\topXX⊤ trains the kernel SVM. The prediction for a new point is f^(x)=∑iα^iyi k(xi,x)+b^\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\,k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}) + \hat bf^​(x)=∑i​α^i​yi​k(xi​,x)+b^, a sum over the support vectors only. The cell repeats the function (so that this notebook is self-contained) and compares it with SVC(kernel="rbf") on the Breast Cancer training set, with γ=0.01\gamma = 0.01γ=0.01 and C=10C = 10C=10 (the values selected below).

def smo(K, y, C, tol=1e-8, max_iter=500_000):
    """Sequential minimal optimization (maximal violating pair) for the SVM dual with a Gram matrix K, labels in {-1, +1} (Section 8.5.2)."""
    n = len(y)
    alpha, G = np.zeros(n), -np.ones(n)
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        e = -y * G
        up = ((y == 1) & (alpha < C)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha > 0))
        low = ((y == 1) & (alpha > 0)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha < C))
        i = np.flatnonzero(up)[np.argmax(e[up])]
        j = np.flatnonzero(low)[np.argmin(e[low])]
        gap = e[i] - e[j]
        if gap <= tol:
            break
        a = max(K[i, i] + K[j, j] - 2 * K[i, j], 1e-12)
        t_i = (C - alpha[i]) if y[i] == 1 else alpha[i]
        t_j = alpha[j] if y[j] == 1 else (C - alpha[j])
        t = min(gap / a, t_i, t_j)
        d_i, d_j = y[i] * t, -y[j] * t
        alpha[i] += d_i
        alpha[j] += d_j
        G += (y * y[i]) * K[:, i] * d_i + (y * y[j]) * K[:, j] * d_j
    e = -y * G
    free = (alpha > 1e-10) & (alpha < C - 1e-10)
    if free.any():
        b = e[free].mean()
    else:
        up = ((y == 1) & (alpha < C)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha > 0))
        low = ((y == 1) & (alpha > 0)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha < C))
        b = (e[up].max() + e[low].min()) / 2
    return alpha, b, it


g_star, C_star = 0.01, 10.0
a_k, b_k, it_k = smo(rbf_kernel(Zb, gamma=g_star), sb, C_star, tol=1e-9)
ref_k = SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=g_star, C=C_star, tol=1e-10).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
dec_mine = rbf_kernel(Zb_te, Zb, gamma=g_star) @ (a_k * sb) + b_k           # f(x) = sum_i alpha_i y_i k(x_i, x) + b
print(f"SMO with the Gaussian Gram matrix: {it_k} iterations, {int((a_k > 1e-9).sum())} support vectors (SVC: {len(ref_k.support_)}), "
      f"largest difference between the test decision functions {np.abs(dec_mine - ref_k.decision_function(Zb_te)).max():.1e}, "
      f"test accuracy {np.mean(np.sign(dec_mine) == sb_te):.4f}")
SMO with the Gaussian Gram matrix: 2084 iterations, 51 support vectors (SVC: 51), largest difference between the test decision functions 3.4e-06, test accuracy 0.9790

9.6.2 Choosing (C,γ)(C, \gamma)(C,γ)¶

The Gaussian SVM has two hyperparameters, and Chapter 5 told us how to choose them: a grid on a logarithmic scale and cross-validation on the training set, with the test set touched once. Figure 9.3 shows the 10-fold cross-validation accuracy on a grid of C∈{10−2,…,103}C\in\{10^{-2}, \dots, 10^3\}C∈{10−2,…,103} and γ∈{10−5,…,10}\gamma\in\{10^{-5}, \dots, 10\}γ∈{10−5,…,10} for the Breast Cancer training set, and the following cell reports the chosen pair, the number of support vectors, the test accuracy and two benchmarks: the linear SVM of Chapter 8 and kkk-nearest neighbors.

skf10 = StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
C_grid, g_grid = 10.0 ** np.arange(-2, 4), 10.0 ** np.arange(-5, 1.01, 1)
search_b = GridSearchCV(SVC(kernel="rbf", tol=1e-4), {"C": C_grid, "gamma": g_grid}, cv=skf10, scoring="accuracy").fit(Zb, yb_tr)
cv_map = search_b.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].reshape(len(C_grid), len(g_grid))        # rows: C, columns: gamma
best_b = search_b.best_estimator_
print(f"best pair of the grid: C = {search_b.best_params_['C']:g}, gamma = {search_b.best_params_['gamma']:g}; 10-fold accuracy {search_b.best_score_:.4f}; "
      f"{len(best_b.support_)} support vectors; test accuracy {best_b.score(Zb_te, yb_te):.4f} ({int((best_b.predict(Zb_te) != yb_te).sum())} errors of {len(yb_te)})")
print(f"cells of the grid within 0.005 of the best accuracy: {int((cv_map >= cv_map.max() - 0.005).sum())} of {cv_map.size}; the majority-class rate is {max(np.mean(yb_tr), 1 - np.mean(yb_tr)):.3f}")
lin_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=0.03, tol=1e-6).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
knn_b = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
pred_rbf, pred_lin = best_b.predict(Zb_te), lin_b.predict(Zb_te)
print(f"benchmarks on the test set: linear SVM (C = 0.03, Chapter 8) {lin_b.score(Zb_te, yb_te):.4f} ({int((pred_lin != yb_te).sum())} errors); 5-NN {knn_b.score(Zb_te, yb_te):.4f}")
only_rbf, only_lin = int(((pred_rbf == yb_te) & (pred_lin != yb_te)).sum()), int(((pred_rbf != yb_te) & (pred_lin == yb_te)).sum())

# Figure 9.3 — 10-fold cross-validation accuracy of the Gaussian SVM on a grid of (gamma, C), Breast Cancer
def figure_9_3():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.6))
    im = ax.imshow(cv_map, origin="lower", cmap="Blues", vmin=0.6, vmax=1.0, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(g_grid)))
    ax.set_xticklabels([f"$10^{{{int(np.log10(g))}}}$" for g in g_grid])
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(C_grid)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([f"$10^{{{int(np.log10(c))}}}$" for c in C_grid])
    for r in range(cv_map.shape[0]):
        for c in range(cv_map.shape[1]):
            ax.text(c, r, f"{cv_map[r, c]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color="white" if cv_map[r, c] > 0.85 else "0.25")
    r_best, c_best = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(cv_map), cv_map.shape)
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((c_best - 0.5, r_best - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, edgecolor=VERMILION, lw=2.5))
    ax.set(xlabel=r"bandwidth $\gamma$", ylabel="$C$", title="10-fold CV accuracy of the Gaussian SVM (Breast Cancer)")
    ax.grid(False)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="accuracy")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_9_3()

The 10-fold accuracy is high in a diagonal band of the plane and falls to the majority-class rate (0.63) on the right. The band says that CCC and γ\gammaγ trade against one another: when γ\gammaγ decreases by a factor of ten the best CCC increases by about the same factor (C=10C = 10C=10 at γ=10−2\gamma = 10^{-2}γ=10−2, C=100C = 100C=100 to 1000 at γ=10−3\gamma = 10^{-3}γ=10−3 and 10-4). A small γ\gammaγ makes the Gaussian kernel nearly constant on the data, the functions of a given norm are then very small, and a large CCC is needed to compensate; the product CγC\gammaCγ is roughly constant along the ridge. The best pair is C=10C = 10C=10, γ=0.01\gamma = 0.01γ=0.01 (10-fold accuracy 0.9765, 51 support vectors) and its test accuracy is 0.979 (3 errors among 143 patients): the same as that of the linear SVM of Chapter 8, which differs from it on one patient in each direction; 5-nearest neighbors makes 6 errors. On the Breast Cancer data, with its 30 features, a nonlinear boundary buys nothing over a linear one, in agreement with Sections 6.7 and 8.8.1; and only 2 of the 42 cells of the grid are within 0.005 of the best, so that one decade of resolution in each parameter is not much finer than needed.

The bandwidth deserves a closer look, because it moves the model through three regimes. The next cell fixes C=10C = 10C=10 and varies γ\gammaγ over eight orders of magnitude, reporting the number of support vectors and the training and test accuracies; Figure 9.4 shows the decision boundaries for three values of γ\gammaγ on two features, the mean radius and the mean texture of Section 8.8.1, where the picture can be drawn.

for g in 10.0 ** np.arange(-5, 1.01, 1):

    rows.append({"gamma": g, "support vectors": len(m_.support_), "training accuracy": m_.score(Zb, yb_tr), "test accuracy": m_.score(Zb_te, yb_te),
                 "predicts one class on the test set": bool(len(np.unique(m_.predict(Zb_te))) == 1)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))

figure_9_4()

The table and Figure 9.4 show the three regimes of γ\gammaγ. For very small γ\gammaγ the model is too rigid (with C=10C = 10C=10 and γ=10−5\gamma = 10^{-5}γ=10−5 the accuracy is only 0.75, because CCC is too small to compensate, as above). Around γ=0.01\gamma = 0.01γ=0.01 the fit is good (51 support vectors, test accuracy 0.979). For γ=0.1\gamma = 0.1γ=0.1 the training accuracy is already 1.000 and the test accuracy falls to 0.951 (170 support vectors). From γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 on we are in the regime of memorization: all 426 training patients are support vectors, the training accuracy is 1.000, and the test accuracy is 0.629, which is the proportion of benign patients in the test set: the model classifies every test patient as benign. The reason is the one of Section 9.3.3 (for γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 the Gram matrix is almost the identity): a new patient is far from every training patient, all the k(xi,x)k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x})k(xi​,x) are close to 0, and the score f^(x)=∑iα^iyik(xi,x)+b^\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_ik(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}) + \hat bf^​(x)=∑i​α^i​yi​k(xi​,x)+b^ reduces to the intercept b^\hat bb^. The same phenomenon explains the picture on two features: for γ=30\gamma = 30γ=30 the decision region is a set of small islands around individual patients (265 support vectors, test accuracy 0.881), and for γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1 the corners of the plot, far from all the data, are labeled by the sign of b^\hat bb^ (the upper left and lower left areas are classified malignant, although there are no malignant patients there): far from the data a Gaussian-kernel model says nothing reliable. With γ=0.05\gamma = 0.05γ=0.05 the boundary is a smooth curve, and slightly better than a line (0.888 against 0.881, Section 8.8.1).

9.6.3 The capacity bound for a kernel classifier¶

Proposition 9.5 says that the margin bound of Theorem 3.7 applies to the kernel SVM with B=∥f^∥H=α^⊤Qα^B = \lVert\hat f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}} = \sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}^\top\mathbf{Q}\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}}B=∥f^​∥H​=α^⊤Qα^​ (with α^\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}α^ the multipliers and Q=diag⁡(y)Kdiag⁡(y)\mathbf{Q} = \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{y})\mathbf{K}\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{y})Q=diag(y)Kdiag(y)) and R=1R = 1R=1 for the Gaussian kernel. (As in Section 8.6.1 the intercept is ignored in BBB, which is a small simplification, and BBB is the value found by the algorithm.) We evaluate the bound on the Breast Cancer training set, with C=10C = 10C=10 and several γ\gammaγ. For the linear kernel the radius R=19.6R = 19.6R=19.6 of one outlier patient made the bound of Section 8.6.1 vacuous; here RRR is 1 by construction, which is the point of the comparison.

conf_b = np.sqrt(np.log(1 / 0.05) / (2 * n_b))                              # delta = 0.05
rows = []
for g in [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1.0]:
    K_ = rbf_kernel(Zb, gamma=g)
    a_, b_, _ = smo(K_, sb, 10.0, tol=1e-7)
    B = np.sqrt((a_ * sb) @ K_ @ (a_ * sb))                                  # ||f||_H
    below = np.mean(sb * (K_ @ (a_ * sb) + b_) < 1 - 1e-6)                   # fraction of training points with margin below 1
    cap = 2 * B * 1.0 / np.sqrt(n_b)                                         # R = 1 for the Gaussian kernel
    test_err = np.mean(np.sign(rbf_kernel(Zb_te, Zb, gamma=g) @ (a_ * sb) + b_) != sb_te)
    rows.append({"gamma": g, "||f||_H": B, "below margin": below, "capacity 2B/sqrt(n)": cap, "bound": below + cap + conf_b, "test error": test_err})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
 gamma  ||f||_H  below margin  capacity 2B/sqrt(n)  bound  test error
 0.000   29.106         0.385                2.820  3.265       0.056
 0.001   19.874         0.174                1.926  2.159       0.035
 0.010   14.358         0.061                1.391  1.512       0.021
 0.100   13.073         0.005                1.267  1.331       0.049
 1.000   19.300         0.000                1.870  1.929       0.371

Near the best γ\gammaγ the norm of the function is ∥f^∥H=13\lVert\hat f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}} = 13∥f^​∥H​=13 to 14, the capacity term 2B/n2B/\sqrt n2B/n​ is 1.3 to 1.4 even with R=1R = 1R=1, and the bound is 1.33 to 1.51: vacuous again, as in Section 8.6.1. The shape is more informative than the level. The bound is large for the two extremes (3.27 for γ=10−4\gamma = 10^{-4}γ=10−4, where 38%38\%38% of the patients are below the margin, and 1.93 for γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1, where the norm grows again to 19), and smallest at γ=0.1\gamma = 0.1γ=0.1 (1.33), where the test error is 4.9%4.9\%4.9%, while the test error is smallest at γ=0.01\gamma = 0.01γ=0.01 (2.1%2.1\%2.1%): the bound locates the good region but not the optimum, which it puts a decade away because the fraction below the margin falls to 0.5%0.5\%0.5% at γ=0.1\gamma = 0.1γ=0.1. At γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1, a model that classifies every test patient as benign (test error 37%37\%37%) has a bound of 1.93, only slightly worse than the good ones: the bound does not see the failure either. Removing the outlier radius did not make the guarantee useful; the capacity term is dominated by BBB, which is large because the SVM with C=10C = 10C=10 pays norm for fit.

9.6.4 Digits: the scale of the features matters for kernels¶

On the Digits data (1347 training and 450 test images, the split of Chapters 6 to 8) we compare the Gaussian SVM with the linear one-vs-one SVM of Chapter 8 and, since it is the most natural reference for a kernel method, the kkk-nearest neighbors of Chapter 4. A point deserves attention: a Gaussian kernel depends on the Euclidean distance between raw feature vectors, so the way in which the pixels are scaled changes the kernel. We tune (C,γ)(C, \gamma)(C,γ) by 5-fold cross-validation for two scalings: the standardization of Chapters 6 to 8 (each of the 64 pixels to zero mean and unit variance), and the division of all the pixels by 16 (the maximum), which keeps all of them on the same scale and does not amplify the pixels that are almost constant.

dg = load_digits()
Xg_tr, Xg_te, yg_tr, yg_te = train_test_split(dg.data, dg.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=dg.target)
skf5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
scale_std = StandardScaler().fit(Xg_tr)
versions = {"standardized pixels": (scale_std.transform(Xg_tr), scale_std.transform(Xg_te)), "pixels / 16": (Xg_tr / 16, Xg_te / 16)}
rows, preds_g = [], {}
for name, (A_tr, A_te) in versions.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    gs_ = GridSearchCV(SVC(kernel="rbf", tol=1e-4), {"C": 10.0 ** np.arange(-1, 4), "gamma": 10.0 ** np.arange(-5, 0.1, 0.5)}, cv=skf5, scoring="accuracy").fit(A_tr, yg_tr)
    preds_g[f"Gaussian SVM, {name}"] = gs_.predict(A_te)
    rows.append({"model": f"Gaussian SVM, {name}", "C": gs_.best_params_["C"], "gamma": gs_.best_params_["gamma"], "5-fold accuracy": gs_.best_score_,
                 "test accuracy": gs_.score(A_te, yg_te), "test errors": int((gs_.predict(A_te) != yg_te).sum()), "support vectors": len(gs_.best_estimator_.support_)})
A_tr, A_te = versions["standardized pixels"]
lin_g = GridSearchCV(SVC(kernel="linear", tol=1e-4), {"C": 10.0 ** np.arange(-4, 1)}, cv=skf5, scoring="accuracy").fit(A_tr, yg_tr)
preds_g["linear SVM (one-vs-one), standardized"] = lin_g.predict(A_te)
rows.append({"model": "linear SVM (one-vs-one), standardized", "C": lin_g.best_params_["C"], "gamma": np.nan, "5-fold accuracy": lin_g.best_score_,
             "test accuracy": lin_g.score(A_te, yg_te), "test errors": int((lin_g.predict(A_te) != yg_te).sum()), "support vectors": len(lin_g.best_estimator_.support_)})

             "test errors": int((knn_g.predict(Xg_te / 16) != yg_te).sum()), "support vectors": np.nan})

        continue

    p_ = binomtest(min(only_a, only_b), only_a + only_b, 0.5).pvalue if only_a + only_b else 1.0

The scaling changes the result. With the standardized pixels the Gaussian SVM makes 11 errors among the 450 test images (0.976; C=1000C = 1000C=1000, γ=0.001\gamma = 0.001γ=0.001, 446 support vectors), and with the pixels divided by 16 it makes 5 (0.989; C=10C = 10C=10, γ=0.316\gamma = 0.316γ=0.316, 713 support vectors); the cross-validation accuracies, 0.984 and 0.991, go in the same direction. A plausible reason, which we have not tested, is that the standardization gives the same weight to the 64 pixels, including the ones near the border of the image that are almost always zero and become huge, standardized, on the rare images where they are not, while the division by 16 leaves the distance dominated by the informative pixels. For the models that we compare: the linear SVM of Chapter 8 makes 9 errors, kkk-nearest neighbors on the pixels divided by 16 makes 7, and the softmax regression of Section 6.6 12. The best Gaussian SVM is a few images better than each of them, but none of these differences is significant (McNemar’s exact p=0.070p = 0.070p=0.070 against the standardized Gaussian SVM, 0.29 against the linear SVM and 0.63 against kkk-NN, with 8, 8 and 4 discordant images). On Digits, a data set that is nearly linearly separable and in which kkk-NN is already good, the kernel is worth a small gain at most, and the choice of the scale of the features matters at least as much as the choice of the kernel.

9.7 Kernel methods at scale¶

9.7.1 What a kernel method costs¶

The price of the kernel trick is paid in nnn. The Gram matrix has n2n^2n2 entries, which must be computed (O(n2d)O(n^2d)O(n2d) operations for the Gaussian kernel) and stored (8n28n^28n2 bytes in double precision: 10,00010{,}00010,000 examples need 0.8 GB and 100,000100{,}000100,000 need 80 GB). Kernel ridge regression solves an n×nn\times nn×n linear system, O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3); the SMO algorithm of Section 8.5.2 takes a number of iterations that grows at least linearly with nnn, each with an O(n)O(n)O(n) update, which gives between O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) and O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) in practice; and the prediction for a new point costs O(nSV d)O(n_{\text{SV}}\,d)O(nSV​d) for the SVM, O(n d)O(n\,d)O(nd) for kernel ridge regression, since every training point is in the sum. For nnn in the thousands this is nothing, and the exact methods are the right choice (Section 9.7.3 will show a case where the exact method is faster than the approximations that match it). For n≥105n\ge 10^5n≥105 they become impractical, and one approximates the kernel by an explicit feature map of moderate dimension DDD, then trains a linear model on it with the methods of Chapter 7, at a cost linear in nnn and in DDD. Two approximations are in common use: random Fourier features, which are data-independent, and the Nyström method, which uses the data.

9.7.2 Random Fourier features¶

A classical theorem of harmonic analysis (Bochner) says that a translation-invariant kernel k(x−z)k(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{z})k(x−z) is the Fourier transform of a positive measure. For the Gaussian kernel the measure is a Gaussian, and the identity can be used as the expectation of a random feature: Rahimi and Recht (2007).

Theorem 9.7 (random Fourier features)

Let k(x,x′)=exp⁡(−γ∥x−x′∥2)k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \exp(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\rVert^2)k(x,x′)=exp(−γ∥x−x′∥2). Draw independent w1,…,wD∼N(0,2γId)\mathbf{w}_1, \dots, \mathbf{w}_D\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, 2\gamma\mathbf{I}_d)w1​,…,wD​∼N(0,2γId​) and b1,…,bD∼Uniform[0,2π]b_1, \dots, b_D\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0, 2\pi]b1​,…,bD​∼Uniform[0,2π], and set

z(x)=2D (cos⁡(wj⊤x+bj))j=1,…,D ∈ RD.\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}) = \sqrt{\tfrac2D}\,\big(\cos(\mathbf{w}_j^\top\mathbf{x} + b_j)\big)_{j = 1, \dots, D}\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^D .z(x)=D2​​(cos(wj⊤​x+bj​))j=1,…,D​ ∈ RD.
(12)

Then (i) E[z(x)⊤z(x′)]=k(x,x′)\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}')\big] = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')E[z(x)⊤z(x′)]=k(x,x′); (ii) for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0,  P(∣z(x)⊤z(x′)−k(x,x′)∣≥ε)≤2e−Dε2/8\ \mathbb{P}\big(\lvert\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}') - k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')\rvert\ge\varepsilon\big)\le 2e^{-D\varepsilon^2/8} P(∣z(x)⊤z(x′)−k(x,x′)∣≥ε)≤2e−Dε2/8; (iii) for mmm points, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ all the m2m^2m2 entries of the approximate Gram matrix are within ε\varepsilonε of the exact ones as soon as D≥8ε2ln⁡2m2δD\ge\frac8{\varepsilon^2}\ln\frac{2m^2}{\delta}D≥ε28​lnδ2m2​.

Proof

(i) Write z(x)⊤z(x′)=1D∑jTj\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}') = \frac1D\sum_jT_jz(x)⊤z(x′)=D1​∑j​Tj​ with Tj=2cos⁡(wj⊤x+bj)cos⁡(wj⊤x′+bj)=cos⁡(wj⊤(x−x′))+cos⁡(wj⊤(x+x′)+2bj)T_j = 2\cos(\mathbf{w}_j^\top\mathbf{x} + b_j)\cos(\mathbf{w}_j^\top\mathbf{x}' + b_j) = \cos\big(\mathbf{w}_j^\top(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')\big) + \cos\big(\mathbf{w}_j^\top(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{x}') + 2b_j\big)Tj​=2cos(wj⊤​x+bj​)cos(wj⊤​x′+bj​)=cos(wj⊤​(x−x′))+cos(wj⊤​(x+x′)+2bj​). Since bjb_jbj​ is uniform on [0,2π][0, 2\pi][0,2π] the expectation of the second term over bjb_jbj​ is 0. The first has the expectation Ecos⁡(w⊤u)=Re⁡ E eiw⊤u=exp⁡(−12u⊤(2γI)u)=e−γ∥u∥2\mathbb{E}\cos(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{u}) = \operatorname{Re}\,\mathbb{E}\,e^{i\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{u}} = \exp\big(-\tfrac12\mathbf{u}^\top(2\gamma\mathbf{I})\mathbf{u}\big) = e^{-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2}Ecos(w⊤u)=ReEeiw⊤u=exp(−21​u⊤(2γI)u)=e−γ∥u∥2 for u=x−x′\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'u=x−x′ (the characteristic function of N(0,2γI)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, 2\gamma\mathbf{I})N(0,2γI)), so E Tj=k(x,x′)\mathbb{E}\,T_j = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')ETj​=k(x,x′). (ii) The TjT_jTj​ are independent with values in [−2,2][-2, 2][−2,2] and mean kkk; Hoeffding’s inequality (Section 3.5) for their average gives P(∣1D∑jTj−k∣≥ε)≤2exp⁡(−2Dε2/42)\mathbb{P}(\lvert\frac1D\sum_jT_j - k\rvert\ge\varepsilon)\le 2\exp(-2D\varepsilon^2/4^2)P(∣D1​∑j​Tj​−k∣≥ε)≤2exp(−2Dε2/42). (iii) A union bound over the m2m^2m2 pairs gives the failure probability 2m2e−Dε2/8≤δ2m^2e^{-D\varepsilon^2/8}\le\delta2m2e−Dε2/8≤δ under the condition on DDD. □\square□

The error of a Fourier feature approximation therefore decreases like 1/D1/\sqrt D1/D​ whatever the dimension ddd and the sample size, a Monte Carlo rate, and independently of the data. For linear models the inner product z(x)⊤z(x′)\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x})^\top\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}')z(x)⊤z(x′) replaces the kernel, and a linear SVM or ridge regression in RD\mathbb{R}^DRD approximates the kernel one.

9.7.3 The Nyström method¶

The second approximation uses m≪nm\ll nm≪n landmark points x~1,…,x~m\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_1, \dots, \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_mx~1​,…,x~m​ (a random subset of the training set) and approximates the Gram matrix of the whole sample by K≈KnmKmm−1Kmn\mathbf{K}\approx\mathbf{K}_{nm}\mathbf{K}_{mm}^{-1}\mathbf{K}_{mn}K≈Knm​Kmm−1​Kmn​, where Knm\mathbf{K}_{nm}Knm​ holds the kernel values between the sample and the landmarks and Kmm\mathbf{K}_{mm}Kmm​ those among the landmarks. It is exact if m=nm = nm=n, and in general it projects the feature space on the span of the images of the landmarks. The explicit feature map is x↦Kmm−1/2 (k(x~j,x))j≤m∈Rm\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{K}_{mm}^{-1/2}\,(k(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j, \mathbf{x}))_{j\le m}\in\mathbb{R}^mx↦Kmm−1/2​(k(x~j​,x))j≤m​∈Rm. It adapts to the data, and it does better than random features with the same number of components when the spectrum of the Gram matrix decays (Figure 9.1(b)).

We compare the two on Digits, with the scaling that worked (pixels divided by 16) and the pair (C,γ)=(10,0.316)(C, \gamma) = (10, 0.316)(C,γ)=(10,0.316) selected in Section 9.6.4. The cell measures, for each number of components, three errors of the approximate Gram matrix on 300 training images (the mean and the largest absolute error of the entries, and the relative Frobenius error), and the test accuracy of a linear SVM trained on the explicit features (with the same CCC; the exact Gaussian SVM has 0.989). First it checks the unbiasedness of Theorem 9.7 on one pair of images.

A_tr, A_te = Xg_tr / 16, Xg_te / 16
g_dig, C_dig = 10 ** -0.5, 10.0
exact_dig = SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=g_dig, C=C_dig, tol=1e-4).fit(A_tr, yg_tr)
acc_exact = exact_dig.score(A_te, yg_te)


def random_fourier_features(X, gamma, D, seed):
    """z(x) = sqrt(2/D) cos(W'x + b), W ~ N(0, 2 gamma I), b ~ U[0, 2 pi]  (Theorem 9.7)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W = rng.normal(0.0, np.sqrt(2 * gamma), size=(X.shape[1], D))
    b = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, size=D)
    return np.sqrt(2.0 / D) * np.cos(X @ W + b)


# (i) unbiasedness and variance for one pair of images
pair = A_tr[:2]
k_pair = float(np.exp(-g_dig * np.sum((pair[0] - pair[1]) ** 2)))
est = np.array([(lambda F: F[0] @ F[1])(random_fourier_features(pair, g_dig, 50, s)) for s in range(4000)])
print(f"one pair of images, D = 50 features, 4000 draws: exact kernel {k_pair:.4f}, mean of the estimates {est.mean():.4f}, "
      f"standard deviation {est.std():.4f} (to be compared with sqrt(1/D) = {np.sqrt(1 / 50):.3f})")

sub = np.arange(300)
K_sub = rbf_kernel(A_tr[sub], gamma=g_dig)
rows = []
for D in [50, 100, 300, 1000, 3000]:
    errs, maxerrs, frob = [], [], []
    for seed in range(5):
        F_ = random_fourier_features(A_tr[sub], g_dig, D, seed)
        errs.append(np.abs(F_ @ F_.T - K_sub).mean())
        maxerrs.append(np.abs(F_ @ F_.T - K_sub).max())
        frob.append(np.linalg.norm(F_ @ F_.T - K_sub) / np.linalg.norm(K_sub))
    F_tr_, F_te_ = random_fourier_features(A_tr, g_dig, D, 0), random_fourier_features(A_te, g_dig, D, 0)
    lin_ = LinearSVC(C=C_dig, max_iter=20_000).fit(F_tr_, yg_tr)
    rows.append({"method": "random Fourier features", "components": D, "mean |error| of K": np.mean(errs), "largest |error| of K": np.mean(maxerrs), "relative Frobenius error": np.mean(frob),
                 "Hoeffding eps (delta = 0.05)": np.sqrt(8 * np.log(2 * 300**2 / 0.05) / D), "test accuracy": lin_.score(F_te_, yg_te)})
for m in [20, 50, 100, 300, 600]:
    ny = Nystroem(gamma=g_dig, n_components=m, random_state=SEED).fit(A_tr)
    F_sub = ny.transform(A_tr[sub])
    lin_ = LinearSVC(C=C_dig, max_iter=20_000).fit(ny.transform(A_tr), yg_tr)
    rows.append({"method": "Nystroem", "components": m, "mean |error| of K": np.abs(F_sub @ F_sub.T - K_sub).mean(), "largest |error| of K": np.abs(F_sub @ F_sub.T - K_sub).max(),
                 "relative Frobenius error": np.linalg.norm(F_sub @ F_sub.T - K_sub) / np.linalg.norm(K_sub), "Hoeffding eps (delta = 0.05)": np.nan, "test accuracy": lin_.score(ny.transform(A_te), yg_te)})
approx = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(approx.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
print(f"exact Gaussian SVM: test accuracy {acc_exact:.4f}, {len(exact_dig.support_)} support vectors out of {len(yg_tr)}")

random Fourier features          50             0.1117                0.5927                    1.0033                        1.5542         0.8200
random Fourier features         100             0.0805                0.4456                    0.7231                        1.0990         0.9200
