# Figure 9.5 — approximating the Gaussian kernel on Digits: random Fourier features and the Nystrom method
def figure_9_5():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.2))
    rf, ny = approx[approx["method"] == "random Fourier features"], approx[approx["method"] == "Nystroem"]
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.loglog(rf["components"], rf["relative Frobenius error"], color=BLUE, marker="o", lw=2, label="random Fourier features")
    ax.loglog(ny["components"], ny["relative Frobenius error"], color=ORANGE, marker="s", lw=2, label="Nyström")
    kk = np.array([50, 3000])
    ax.loglog(kk, rf["relative Frobenius error"].iloc[0] * np.sqrt(kk[0] / kk), color="0.4", ls=":", lw=1.5, label=r"slope $-1/2$")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of components ($D$ or $m$)", ylabel="relative Frobenius error of the Gram matrix", title="(a) error of the kernel")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.semilogx(rf["components"], rf["test accuracy"], color=BLUE, marker="o", lw=2, label="random Fourier features")
    ax.semilogx(ny["components"], ny["test accuracy"], color=ORANGE, marker="s", lw=2, label="Nyström")
    ax.axhline(acc_exact, color="k", ls="--", lw=1.4, label="exact Gaussian SVM")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of components ($D$ or $m$)", ylabel="test accuracy", ylim=(0.8, 1.0), title="(b) accuracy of a linear SVM on the features")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_9_5()

Theorem 9.7 is visible in the first line: for one pair of images, with D=50D = 50D=50 features, the average of 4000 independent estimates is 0.0802 for an exact kernel value of 0.0804 (unbiased), with a standard deviation of 0.143, of the order of 1/D=0.141\sqrt{1/D} = 0.1411/D​=0.141. The errors of the Fourier approximation decrease like D−1/2D^{-1/2}D−1/2 (Figure 9.5(a): the relative Frobenius error goes from 1.00 at D=50D = 50D=50 to 0.13 at D=3000D = 3000D=3000, a factor 7.7=607.7 = \sqrt{60}7.7=60​ for a factor 60 in DDD), and the Hoeffding value ε\varepsilonε of the theorem, which holds with probability 0.95 for all the entries at once, is conservative by a factor of about 2.5 against the largest observed error (0.35 against 0.14 at D=1000D = 1000D=1000). The test accuracy of the linear SVM on the Fourier features is 0.92 with D=100D = 100D=100, 0.980 with D=1000D = 1000D=1000 and 0.984 with D=3000D = 3000D=3000, against 0.989 for the exact Gaussian SVM: about a thousand features are needed to come within one percent. The Nyström method reaches the same accuracy with about ten times fewer components: 0.973 with m=50m = 50m=50, 0.987 with m=100m = 100m=100 and 0.989 at m=600m = 600m=600, although its Gram matrix is far from exact: the relative Frobenius error is still 0.11 at m=600m = 600m=600 and the largest entry error is large (0.7 to 1.0, on the diagonal, where a low-rank matrix cannot reproduce the unit diagonal of a kernel that is almost the identity for γ=0.316\gamma = 0.316γ=0.316). The accuracy of the classifier needs less than an accurate Gram matrix: what matters is that the span of the features contain a good classifier. Finally, the comparison of cost deserves a warning. For n=1347n = 1347n=1347 the exact SVM trains faster than the approximations that match it (the Gram matrix has 1.8 million entries): kernel approximations are for data sets with nnn of the order of 105 or more, where the exact Gram matrix cannot even be stored.

9.8 Designing kernels¶

A kernel encodes what “similar” means for the data at hand, and Proposition 9.2 gives a recipe book for building new ones from known ones, which will be valid by construction. Sums of kernels act on different groups of features or different views of the data (a sum of kernels is a kernel on the concatenated feature spaces); products combine conditions; normalizing k(x,z)/k(x,x)k(z,z)k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})/\sqrt{k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})k(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z})}k(x,z)/k(x,x)k(z,z)​ gives a kernel with unit images; and the same machinery covers inputs that are not vectors (strings, graphs, trees, images), where the kernel is the way of introducing the knowledge about the problem (Chapter 17 and Chapter 21 will meet some of them, in the guise of convolutions and graph Laplacians).

In scikit-learn any kernel can be used with SVC(kernel="precomputed"): the training matrix K\mathbf{K}K is passed to fit, and the matrix of the kernel values between the test and the training points to predict. The first thing to check is that nothing changes with a built-in kernel. The second is an illustration of Proposition 9.2 on the Breast Cancer data, whose 30 features are the mean, the standard error and the worst value of ten measurements: we compare the Gaussian kernel on all the features, the sum of three Gaussian kernels, one for each group of ten features, and their product (which by Proposition 9.2(ii) and the factorization of the exponential is exactly the Gaussian kernel on all the features, if the bandwidth is the same).

K_tr_pre = rbf_kernel(Zb, gamma=g_star)
pre_svc = SVC(kernel="precomputed", C=C_star, tol=1e-10).fit(K_tr_pre, yb_tr)
builtin = SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=g_star, C=C_star, tol=1e-10).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
diff_pre = np.abs(pre_svc.decision_function(rbf_kernel(Zb_te, Zb, gamma=g_star)) - builtin.decision_function(Zb_te)).max()
print(f"precomputed kernel against the built-in Gaussian kernel: largest difference of the decision functions {diff_pre:.1e}")

groups = [slice(0, 10), slice(10, 20), slice(20, 30)]                       # mean, standard error, worst value


def k_single(A, B, g):
    return rbf_kernel(A, B, gamma=g)


def k_sum(A, B, g):
    return sum(rbf_kernel(A[:, s], B[:, s], gamma=g) for s in groups)


def k_product(A, B, g):
    return np.prod([rbf_kernel(A[:, s], B[:, s], gamma=g) for s in groups], axis=0)


rows = []
for name, kern in [("Gaussian on all 30 features", k_single), ("sum of three Gaussians (one per group)", k_sum), ("product of three Gaussians", k_product)]:
    best = None
    for g in [0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3]:
        K_ = kern(Zb, Zb, g)
        for C in [0.1, 1, 10, 100]:
            accs = []
            for tr, va in skf10.split(Zb, yb_tr):
                m_ = SVC(kernel="precomputed", C=C, tol=1e-4).fit(K_[np.ix_(tr, tr)], yb_tr[tr])
                accs.append(m_.score(K_[np.ix_(va, tr)], yb_tr[va]))
            if best is None or np.mean(accs) > best[0]:
                best = (np.mean(accs), g, C)
    acc_cv, g, C = best
    K_ = kern(Zb, Zb, g)
    final = SVC(kernel="precomputed", C=C, tol=1e-6).fit(K_, yb_tr)
    rows.append({"kernel": name, "gamma": g, "C": C, "10-fold accuracy": acc_cv, "test accuracy": final.score(kern(Zb_te, Zb, g), yb_te),
                 "smallest eigenvalue of the Gram matrix": np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_).min()})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))
g_cmp = 0.03
print(f"product kernel against the Gaussian kernel on all the features (same gamma = {g_cmp}): largest difference of the Gram matrices "
      f"{np.abs(k_product(Zb, Zb, g_cmp) - k_single(Zb, Zb, g_cmp)).max():.1e}")
precomputed kernel against the built-in Gaussian kernel: largest difference of the decision functions 5.7e-14

                                kernel  gamma  C  10-fold accuracy  test accuracy  smallest eigenvalue of the Gram matrix
           Gaussian on all 30 features   0.03  1            0.9789          0.979                               0.0005383
sum of three Gaussians (one per group)   0.03 10            0.9765          0.965                               2.574e-05
            product of three Gaussians   0.03  1            0.9789          0.979                               0.0005383
product kernel against the Gaussian kernel on all the features (same gamma = 0.03): largest difference of the Gram matrices 1.7e-15

The precomputed kernel reproduces the built-in one to 7⋅10−147\cdot 10^{-14}7⋅10−14. The experiment on the groups confirms the algebra of Proposition 9.2: the product of the three Gaussian kernels is exactly the Gaussian kernel on the 30 features (the Gram matrices differ by 2⋅10−152\cdot 10^{-15}2⋅10−15, and the tuned models are identical: 10-fold accuracy 0.9789 and test accuracy 0.979), because e−γ∥x−z∥2=∏ge−γ∥xg−zg∥2e^{-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{z}\rVert^2} = \prod_ge^{-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x}_g - \mathbf{z}_g\rVert^2}e−γ∥x−z∥2=∏g​e−γ∥xg​−zg​∥2. The sum is a different kernel (it adds the three feature spaces instead of multiplying them: a function that is a sum of functions of the groups) and it is valid, with a positive smallest eigenvalue (2.6⋅10−52.6\cdot 10^{-5}2.6⋅10−5), but it is not better on these data: 10-fold accuracy 0.9765 and test accuracy 0.965 against 0.9789 and 0.979 (2 more errors among 143 patients, within the noise). Prior knowledge is only useful when it is correct, and here the correct statement is that the three groups are strongly redundant (the mean and the worst value of a measurement carry nearly the same information, Section 6.2.4).

9.9 Summary¶

  • Kernels. A kernel is an inner product in a feature space, k(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) = \langle\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\ranglek(x,z)=⟨ϕ(x),ϕ(z)⟩, and the kernel trick replaces xi⊤xj\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jxi⊤​xj​ by k(xi,xj)k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)k(xi​,xj​) in every algorithm that uses the data only through inner products: ridge regression (Proposition 6.12), the SVM (Chapter 8), and the SMO algorithm, which ran unchanged on a Gaussian Gram matrix (2,0942{,}0942,094 iterations, the 51 support vectors of SVC). The kernel defines distances and angles in the feature space: ∥ϕ(x)−ϕ(z)∥2=k(x,x)+k(z,z)−2k(x,z)\lVert\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}) - \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\rVert^2 = k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}) + k(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}) - 2k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z})∥ϕ(x)−ϕ(z)∥2=k(x,x)+k(z,z)−2k(x,z).

  • Which functions are kernels (Theorem 9.1, Proposition 9.2). A symmetric function is a kernel if and only if all its Gram matrices are positive semidefinite; sums, products, positive scalings, polynomials with non-negative coefficients and exponentials of kernels are kernels, hence so are the polynomial and the Gaussian kernels. On the 150 Iris flowers the Gram matrices have the ranks 4 (linear), 35 (cubic polynomial, =(73)=\binom{7}{3}=(37​)) and 149 (Gaussian: the number of distinct flowers), while tanh⁡(x⊤z)\tanh(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z})tanh(x⊤z) and the distance have 74 and 148 negative eigenvalues: they are not kernels. The Gaussian kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (explicit in one dimension: fifteen features reproduce it to 2⋅10−52\cdot 10^{-5}2⋅10−5), and its parameter γ\gammaγ sets the effective dimension seen by a sample (on the 426 Breast Cancer patients, between 8 and 426 eigenvalues above 10-3 of the largest).

  • The representer theorem (Theorem 9.4). For any loss that depends on the values of fff on the sample and any strictly increasing penalty of ∥f∥H\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}∥f∥H​, the minimizer over the RKHS is f=∑iαik(⋅,xi)f = \sum_i\alpha_ik(\cdot, \mathbf{x}_i)f=∑i​αi​k(⋅,xi​), with f(xj)=(Kα)jf(\mathbf{x}_j) = (\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha)_jf(xj​)=(Kα)j​ and ∥f∥2=α⊤Kα\lVert f\rVert^2 = \boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha∥f∥2=α⊤Kα: an infinite-dimensional problem becomes a problem in nnn coefficients. Ridge, SVM, logistic regression and SVR are instances. The complexity of the class is controlled by ∥f∥H\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}∥f∥H​ and R=sup⁡k(x,x)R = \sup\sqrt{k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x})}R=supk(x,x)​, not by the dimension (Proposition 9.5): Theorem 3.7 applies in the feature space.

  • Kernel ridge regression (Proposition 9.6). α^=(K+λI)−1y\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y}α^=(K+λI)−1y; the eigenvectors of K\mathbf{K}K are shrunk by μj/(μj+λ)\mu_j/(\mu_j + \lambda)μj​/(μj​+λ), the singular-value view of Chapter 6; the leave-one-out error is ei/(1−Hii)e_i/(1 - H_{ii})ei​/(1−Hii​) (checked against 331 refits to 10-12). On Diabetes the Gaussian kernel has the same leave-one-out RMSE as ridge (55.5), and a test RMSE of 51.7 to 52.4 against 53.3 that the data cannot confirm.

  • Kernel SVM (Section 9.6). (C,γ)(C, \gamma)(C,γ) are tuned on a logarithmic grid by cross-validation; the good region is a diagonal band (CγC\gammaCγ roughly constant for small γ\gammaγ). The bandwidth has three regimes: nearly linear, good, and memorization (for γ≥1\gamma\ge 1γ≥1 on Breast Cancer all the 426 patients are support vectors, the training accuracy is 1 and the model classifies every test patient as benign: far from the data the score reduces to the intercept). On Breast Cancer the best Gaussian SVM (C=10C = 10C=10, γ=0.01\gamma = 0.01γ=0.01, test accuracy 0.979) is as good as the linear SVM, and on Digits it makes 5 errors in 450 with the pixels divided by 16 against 11 with the standardized pixels, but no difference with the linear SVM (9) or kkk-NN (7) is significant: the scale of the features matters for a kernel at least as much as the kernel itself. The capacity bound is vacuous (1.3 to 1.5 near the best γ\gammaγ, even with R=1R = 1R=1) but ranks the extremes correctly.

  • Scaling up (Section 9.7). Gram matrix O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) in memory, O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) for kernel ridge regression. Random Fourier features are unbiased and their error decreases like D−1/2D^{-1/2}D−1/2 (Theorem 9.7); the Nyström method uses the data and needs about ten times fewer components. On Digits 1000 Fourier features come within one percent of the exact SVM (0.980 against 0.989), and 100 Nyström landmarks are about as good (0.987); but at n=1347n = 1347n=1347 the exact method is the cheaper one: approximations pay for nnn in the tens of thousands.

  • Designing kernels (Section 9.8). Sums and products of kernels are kernels; a product of Gaussian kernels on groups of features with the same bandwidth is exactly the Gaussian kernel on all of them (difference 10-16), while a sum of kernels per group was not better than the single kernel on Breast Cancer.

Data sources¶

  • Iris: R. A. Fisher, “The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems”, Annals of Eugenics 7(2), 179–188 (1936). Bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn. The target is recoded so that malignant =+1= +1=+1; the training and test sets are the stratified split of Chapters 6 to 8.

  • Digits: E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, “Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits”, UCI Machine Learning Repository (1998). The test portion of the data set, 1,797 images of 8×88\times 88×8 pixels, is bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Diabetes: B. Efron, T. Hastie, I. Johnstone and R. Tibshirani, “Least Angle Regression”, Annals of Statistics 32(2), 407–499 (2004). Bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Constructed data (flagged in the text): the three points of Worked example 9.1 and the small data sets of the manual exercises. All the experiments of the chapter use the real data sets above.

Further reading¶

  • B. Schölkopf and A. J. Smola, Learning with Kernels, MIT Press, 2002. The reference on kernel methods: positive definite kernels, RKHS, the representer theorem, SVMs, kernel PCA.

  • J. Shawe-Taylor and N. Cristianini, Kernel Methods for Pattern Analysis, Cambridge University Press, 2004. Kernels, their construction and their statistical analysis, with many examples of kernels for structured data.

  • N. Aronszajn, “Theory of reproducing kernels”, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 68(3), 337–404 (1950). The origin of the RKHS and the Moore–Aronszajn theorem.

  • G. Kimeldorf and G. Wahba, “Some results on Tchebycheffian spline functions”, Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications 33(1), 82–95 (1971), and B. Schölkopf, R. Herbrich and A. J. Smola, “A generalized representer theorem”, COLT 2001. The representer theorem in its original and in its general form (Theorem 9.4).

  • C. A. Micchelli, “Interpolation of scattered data: distance matrices and conditionally positive definite functions”, Constructive Approximation 2, 11–22 (1986). Positive definiteness of the Gaussian kernel (Section 9.3.3).

  • A. Rahimi and B. Recht, “Random features for large-scale kernel machines”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 20, 2007 (Theorem 9.7), and C. K. I. Williams and M. Seeger, “Using the Nyström method to speed up kernel machines”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 13, 2001.

  • C. E. Rasmussen and C. K. I. Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press, 2006 (free online). The Bayesian view of the same objects: kernel ridge regression is the posterior mean of a Gaussian process with covariance kkk (a natural continuation of Section 6.3.5).

  • M. Hein and O. Bousquet, “Kernels, associated structures and generalizations”, Max Planck Institute Technical Report 127 (2004), and T. Hofmann, B. Schölkopf and A. J. Smola, “Kernel methods in machine learning”, Annals of Statistics 36(3), 1171–1220 (2008). Surveys.

  • T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009, Chapter 5 (smoothing splines and RKHS) and Chapter 12.

9.10 Exercises¶

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in Appendix C.

Manual (analytical) exercises¶

Exercise 9.1 ★ — Kernel or not? For each function on R\mathbb{R}R (or on (0,∞)(0, \infty)(0,∞) where indicated) decide whether it is a kernel, with a proof or a counterexample: (a) k(x,z)=(xz)2k(x, z) = (xz)^2k(x,z)=(xz)2; (b) k(x,z)=−(x−z)2k(x, z) = -(x - z)^2k(x,z)=−(x−z)2; (c) k(x,z)=cos⁡(x−z)k(x, z) = \cos(x - z)k(x,z)=cos(x−z); (d) k(x,z)=max⁡(x,z)k(x, z) = \max(x, z)k(x,z)=max(x,z) on (0,∞)(0, \infty)(0,∞); (e) k(x,z)=min⁡(x,z)k(x, z) = \min(x, z)k(x,z)=min(x,z) on (0,∞)(0, \infty)(0,∞).

Hint. To prove that a function is a kernel, give a feature map or use Proposition 9.2; to refute it, find a 2×22\times 22×2 Gram matrix with a negative eigenvalue or determinant. For (c) use cos⁡(x−z)=cos⁡xcos⁡z+sin⁡xsin⁡z\cos(x - z) = \cos x\cos z + \sin x\sin zcos(x−z)=cosxcosz+sinxsinz; for (e) write min⁡(x,z)=∫0∞I[t≤x] I[t≤z] dt\min(x, z) = \int_0^\infty\mathbb{I}[t\le x]\,\mathbb{I}[t\le z]\,dtmin(x,z)=∫0∞​I[t≤x]I[t≤z]dt.

Python (computational) exercises¶

Exercise 9.6 ★ — Testing kernels numerically. Write a function that returns the smallest eigenvalue of a Gram matrix (symmetrized) relative to the largest one. Apply it to the first 200 standardized patients of the Breast Cancer training set for: the linear, polynomial (degree 2, c=1c = 1c=1), Gaussian and Laplacian kernels; the cosine similarity x⊤z/(∥x∥∥z∥)\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z}/(\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{z}\rVert)x⊤z/(∥x∥∥z∥); tanh⁡(γx⊤z+c)\tanh(\gamma\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + c)tanh(γx⊤z+c) for three values of ccc; and the histogram-intersection function ∑lmin⁡(xl,zl)\sum_l\min(x_l, z_l)∑l​min(xl​,zl​) applied to the non-standardized features divided by their maxima. Which ones are kernels? For those that are not, how negative is the smallest eigenvalue?

Hint. np.linalg.eigvalsh; a relative threshold of 10-10 separates rounding errors from real negative eigenvalues. The histogram intersection is a kernel on non-negative features (it is the sum over the coordinates of min⁡(xl,zl)\min(x_l, z_l)min(xl​,zl​), each a kernel by Exercise 9.1(e)).

Exercise 9.7 ★★ — Kernel ridge regression and the Laplacian kernel. Reproduce the table of Section 9.5.2 for the Diabetes data with loo_grid, and repeat the experiment with the Laplacian kernel exp⁡(−γ∥x−z∥1)\exp(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{z}\rVert_1)exp(−γ∥x−z∥1​) on a grid of γ\gammaγ. Compare the leave-one-out RMSE, the effective degrees of freedom and the test RMSE of the best Gaussian and the best Laplacian model, and check your KRR against KernelRidge of scikit-learn (whose alpha is our λ\lambdaλ).

Hint. laplacian_kernel(Z, gamma=g); for KernelRidge use kernel="precomputed" with alpha=lam and center the response yourself (KernelRidge has no intercept).

Exercise 9.8 ★★ — Scale and bandwidth on Wine. On the Wine data (load_wine; 178 wines, 13 chemical measurements, 3 cultivars) with a stratified split of 75%/25%75\%/25\%75%/25%, tune (C,γ)(C, \gamma)(C,γ) of a Gaussian SVM by 5-fold cross-validation on the raw features, on the standardized features and on the features divided by their maximum, with the grid of Section 9.6.2. Draw the three cross-validation maps, and report the best pairs, the test accuracies and the number of support vectors. Explain the difference between the raw and the standardized features by the scales of the features (look at the standard deviations).

Hint. StandardScaler fitted on the training set only; the proline has a scale of hundreds and the hue of tenths.

Exercise 9.9 ★★★ — The price of approximating. On Digits (pixels divided by 16), for γ∈{0.03,0.1,0.316}\gamma\in\{0.03, 0.1, 0.316\}γ∈{0.03,0.1,0.316} (with C=10C = 10C=10), compare the exact Gaussian SVM with Nyström features and with random Fourier features for m,D∈{25,50,100,200,400,800}m, D\in\{25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800\}m,D∈{25,50,100,200,400,800}: report the mean absolute error of the Gram matrix on 300 images and the test accuracy of a linear SVM on the features. How do the two approximations depend on γ\gammaγ? What is the smallest number of components for which each stays within 0.5%0.5\%0.5% of the accuracy of the exact SVM?

Hint. Nystroem(gamma=..., n_components=...) and RBFSampler(gamma=..., n_components=...) of sklearn.kernel_approximation; a larger γ\gammaγ means a more slowly decaying spectrum (Figure 9.1(b)), which is harder for the low-rank Nyström approximation.

Exercise 9.10 ★★★ — Your own kernel. On Digits (pixels divided by 16), build with sklearn.metrics.pairwise the χ2\chi^2χ2 kernel (chi2_kernel) and the sum of a Gaussian and a linear kernel, check that their Gram matrices are positive semidefinite, tune (C,γ)(C, \gamma)(C,γ) for each by 5-fold cross-validation with precomputed kernels, and compare their test accuracies with that of the Gaussian kernel of Section 9.6.4 by McNemar’s test. Is there an advantage in a kernel designed for non-negative histograms?

Hint. SVC(kernel="precomputed"); build the training matrix once per γ\gammaγ and slice it for the folds, as in Section 9.8. The χ2\chi^2χ2 kernel is exp⁡(−γ∑l(xl−zl)2/(xl+zl))\exp(-\gamma\sum_l(x_l - z_l)^2/(x_l + z_l))exp(−γ∑l​(xl​−zl​)2/(xl​+zl​)).

What comes next¶

We can now fit rich nonlinear models with the machinery of convex optimization, and we know why they work: the regularization controls the norm in a feature space whose dimension does not matter. Two questions remain open in Part II. The first is sparsity in the features: the SVM is sparse in the examples (the support vectors), but its weight vector, and that of ridge, use all the coordinates; Chapter 10 replaces the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty by the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm, for which the representer theorem does not hold, and which sets coefficients exactly to zero (the lasso, with the proximal and coordinate methods that solve it, relatives of the algorithms of Sections 7.6 and 8.5). The second is nonlinear models that are not based on distances: Chapter 11 studies decision trees and ensembles, which deal with features of any scale and with interactions without any kernel, at the cost of the convex structure; the probabilities that they produce will need the recalibration of Section 8.7.3. In Part III, Chapter 13 returns to the Gram matrix: the eigendecomposition of the centered K\mathbf{K}K is kernel PCA, and the shrinkage of the eigenvalues of Section 9.5 will be seen as a projection on the leading components. And in Part IV the first layer of a neural network is, in a precise sense, a randomly or adaptively chosen feature map: the random Fourier features of Section 9.7 are a two-layer network with random first-layer weights and a cosine activation, and the question that Chapters 14 and 15 will take up is what is gained by learning it.
